questions.stem: All monitors are functioning during a stable MAC case, but the CRNA steps out of the room briefly. Which requirement of ASA Standard I is no longer met?
options: Continuous waveform capnography with audible alarms
Pulse oximetry with a variable-pitch tone
The ECG with ST-segment analysis enabled
questions.explanation: ASA Standard I requires qualified anesthesia personnel in the room throughout every general anesthetic, regional anesthetic, and MAC, so a full set of working monitors does not satisfy it when the provider leaves. Capnography, the variable-pitch pulse tone, and the ECG belong to Standard II, which is still being met here.

questions.stem: A 3-hour open laparotomy has continuous ECG, SpO2, ETCO2, and BP every 5 minutes, but no temperature data. Which ASA Standard II domain is missing?
questions.explanation: ASA Standard II requires continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature, and temperature must be monitored when changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected. A 3-hour open laparotomy loses heat through the exposed abdomen and fluid shifts, so the missing domain here is temperature, while ECG, SpO2, ETCO2, and BP cover the other three.

questions.stem: During stable GA without an arterial catheter, the NIBP cuff is changed from cycling every 5 minutes to every 10 minutes because repeated readings are normal. Which statement is correct?
options: Acceptable while ECG and SpO2 run continuously
Violates the 5-minute minimum for BP and HR
Acceptable after three stable pressures in a row
Acceptable unless vasoactive drugs are running
questions.explanation: ASA Standard II requires arterial blood pressure and heart rate to be determined and evaluated at least every 5 minutes; measurement may be more frequent but never less. Continuous ECG and oximetry do not substitute for the pressure measurement, and stable readings or the absence of vasoactive drugs do not relax the interval.

questions.stem: Beyond ECG and blood pressure, which FOUR methods satisfy ASA 2.3 for evaluating circulation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: ASA 2.3 says circulation is evaluated by at least one of pulse palpation, auscultation of heart sounds, an intra-arterial pressure tracing, ultrasound peripheral pulse monitoring, or pulse plethysmography or oximetry, in addition to ECG and blood pressure. Hourly urine output and skin temperature reflect perfusion indirectly but are not listed methods.

questions.stem: During prone positioning after induction, ECG electrodes are removed and not replaced for 10 minutes while pulse oximetry and NIBP continue. Which requirement is specifically unmet?
options: ECG reserved for patients with heart disease
ECG required from skin incision until closure
Continuous ECG from start of anesthesia to leaving
ECG required just at induction and at emergence
questions.explanation: ASA Standard II requires the ECG to be continuously displayed from the beginning of anesthesia until preparing to leave the anesthetizing location, regardless of cardiac history. Prone repositioning is a high-risk moment for arrhythmias and line problems, so a 10-minute gap violates the standard even with oximetry and NIBP running.

questions.stem: During every general anesthetic using an anesthesia machine, which oxygen-safety monitor is specifically required?
options: An O2 analyzer in the breathing system with a low-O2 alarm
Arterial blood gases at least once per hour of anesthesia
A pulse oximeter with an alarm set to 90% or lower
A paramagnetic analyzer placed in the expiratory limb
questions.explanation: During general anesthesia with an anesthesia machine, ASA requires an oxygen analyzer measuring inspired concentration in the breathing system with a low-concentration limit alarm, which catches hypoxic gas delivery before the patient desaturates. Pulse oximetry is required separately, and arterial blood gases are not a standard requirement.

questions.stem: During GA, inspired O2 is 50% and expired O2 is 45% with stable ventilation. What best explains the difference?
options: A circuit leak drawing in room air
Expected oxygen uptake by the patient
Hypoxic gas delivery from the machine
questions.explanation: Expired oxygen is lower than inspired oxygen because the patient takes up oxygen in the lungs, and a 5% gap is typical with stable ventilation. A circuit leak drawing in room air would lower the inspired value instead, and a failing analyzer or hypoxic gas would show an abnormal inspired reading.

questions.stem: During GA with an ETT, capnography alarms repeatedly and the provider considers relying only on chest rise and breath sounds. What does ASA 2.2 require?
options: Expired CO2 just at intubation and extubation
Clinical signs by themselves are adequate
Expired CO2 once SpO2 falls below 92%
Continual expired CO2 plus clinical signs
questions.explanation: ASA 2.2 requires continual monitoring of expired CO2 from placement of an ETT or supraglottic device until removal, in addition to clinical signs such as chest excursion and breath sounds. Frequent alarms call for troubleshooting the sampling line or the patient, not abandoning capnography, and waiting for desaturation defeats its purpose.

questions.stem: The first case on Monday follows a weekend in which the machine was left with high oxygen flow running. What is the main hazard if desflurane is used without changing the absorbent?
options: Rebreathing from a stuck expiratory valve
Hypoxic mixture from the oxygen pipeline
questions.explanation: Fresh gas flowing through the absorber over a weekend dries it out, and desflurane, and to a lesser extent isoflurane, reacting with desiccated strong-base absorbent produces carbon monoxide; sevoflurane with dry absorbent can generate heat and even fire. The absorbent should be replaced. Compound A is a concern with sevoflurane at low flows, not a desiccation product of desflurane.

questions.stem: Which patients most clearly require temperature monitoring under ASA 2.4: a 15-minute knee scope, a 4-hour open colectomy, and a cardiac case with planned cooling?
options: The knee scope and the cardiac case
The colectomy and the cardiac case
The colectomy alone, since perfusion tracks cooling
questions.explanation: ASA 2.4 requires temperature monitoring when clinically significant changes in body temperature are intended, anticipated, or suspected. A 4-hour open colectomy is expected to cause heat loss, and planned cooling on bypass is an intended change, so both need it. A 15-minute knee scope does not, and perfusion monitoring does not replace the anesthesia record of temperature.

questions.stem: Rocuronium was given, but no twitch monitor is used and extubation is based only on a 5-second head lift. Which AANA monitoring expectation is not met?
options: NM monitoring when reversal will not be given
NM monitoring for cases over 2 hours
questions.explanation: AANA standards call for monitoring the neuromuscular response to assess depth of blockade and degree of recovery whenever neuromuscular blockers are used, with quantitative monitoring when available. A 5-second head lift can be achieved with a TOF ratio well below 0.9, so it does not exclude residual blockade.

questions.stem: Before reversing rocuronium, which method gives the most reliable evidence of neuromuscular recovery?
options: A sustained 5-second head lift off the pillow
A visual train-of-four count at the ulnar nerve
Tactile assessment of fade during tetanus
questions.explanation: Quantitative monitors such as acceleromyography or electromyography measure the TOF ratio directly, and recovery to a ratio of at least 0.9 is the target before extubation. Visual and tactile assessment cannot detect fade once the ratio exceeds about 0.4, and a head lift can be sustained with significant residual block.

questions.stem: A patient under deep sedation becomes progressively hypercapnic while SpO2 remains normal on supplemental oxygen. Which monitoring failure most closely mirrors the recurring problem identified in hypoventilation closed claims?
options: Failure to obtain intermittent arterial blood gases
Failure to use invasive blood pressure monitoring
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen can preserve SpO2 despite progressively inadequate ventilation, so pulse oximetry may not reveal early hypoventilation. Monitoring ventilation, including exhaled CO2 when indicated, detects the problem before oxygen desaturation necessarily occurs.

questions.stem: Critical-incident studies of preventable anesthesia mishaps identified which factor as the most common contributor?
options: Human error rather than equipment failure
Drug allergy that could not be predicted
questions.explanation: Critical-incident studies, beginning with Cooper's work, found that most preventable mishaps involved human error such as drug or breathing circuit mistakes, while pure equipment failure was a small minority. That finding drove checklists, standardized equipment, and monitoring standards. Unpredictable disease progression or allergy would not count as preventable.

questions.stem: Which category of event is the most common preventable source of anesthesia claims and payouts?
questions.explanation: In the ASA Closed Claims Project, adverse respiratory events such as inadequate ventilation, esophageal intubation, and difficult intubation were historically the largest source of claims involving death or brain damage, and many were judged preventable with better monitoring. Pulse oximetry and capnography reduced their share, but they remain a leading category.

questions.stem: Immediately after intubation, bilateral chest movement appears present and SpO2 remains 100% from preoxygenation, but no sustained exhaled CO2 waveform appears. Which safety advance is designed to prevent the catastrophic error most associated with this pattern?
options: Processed EEG to detect intraoperative awareness
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation can keep SpO2 normal for minutes even when the tube is in the esophagus, and chest movement can mislead. Sustained exhaled CO2 provides the routine confirmation that ventilation is reaching the lungs, which is why capnography sharply reduced claims for unrecognized esophageal intubation.

questions.stem: An overnight provider has been awake 20 hours, loud music is playing, and phone use occurs between vital checks. Which THREE factors impair vigilance? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Vigilance falls with external distractions such as loud music and noise, human factors such as fatigue and circadian disruption, and self-initiated distractions such as phone use. Continuous capnography alarms, a systematic monitor sweep, and quantitative neuromuscular monitoring support vigilance rather than impairing it.

questions.stem: After a hypoxic event, the team initially attributes the problem to a ventilator defect, but testing shows normal equipment function and review reveals an incomplete pre-use check. Which closed-claims lesson BEST applies?
options: Equipment checks add little since failures are random
Device malfunction is the usual cause of adverse events
A normal post-event test rules out any equipment role
User error and skipped checks outnumber device failure
questions.explanation: Closed claims analyses show that true device malfunction is rare, while misuse, unfamiliarity, and failure to perform the pre-use check account for most equipment-related harm. A normal test after the event points toward use error, which is why a complete pre-use checkout before each case matters.

questions.stem: A preventable event follows incorrect use of the anesthesia workstation rather than failure of the device itself. Which equipment category has been disproportionately represented in closed claims from misuse?
questions.explanation: In closed claims involving gas delivery equipment, misuse such as incorrect setup or failure to check produced far more claims than true device failure, and gas delivery systems were the equipment category most often involved. Infusion pumps, NIBP cuffs, and warming devices appear in claims less often.

questions.stem: A provider who has never used a new ventilator starts the case without testing the machine, because it worked yesterday. Which two human factors most commonly underlie equipment mishaps?
questions.explanation: Equipment-related mishaps most often come from users who are unfamiliar with a device and skip the pre-use check, rather than from manufacturer defects or electrical problems. Training on each machine model and a full checkout before use address both causes.

questions.stem: The first case of the day begins without testing the workstation, because the machine worked normally overnight. Which AANA requirement is most directly violated?
options: Continuous provider presence in the room
questions.explanation: AANA standards require verifying the function of anesthesia equipment before each anesthetic, so normal function the night before does not replace the morning checkout. Leaks, empty cylinders, or exhausted absorbent can develop between cases, and the first case of the day typically gets the full check.

questions.stem: SpO2 alarm volume is muted and the low limit is set to 70%. Which AANA standard is violated?
questions.explanation: AANA Standard 9 requires alarms for monitored variables to be set to appropriate limits and kept audible, so a muted SpO2 tone with a 70% low limit violates it. Equipment verification and neuromuscular monitoring fall under other standards, and the preoperative evaluation is unrelated to alarm settings.

questions.stem: During surgery, the pulse-oximeter tone progressively drops in pitch while the provider is looking at the surgical field. What information is being conveyed before the numerical SpO2 is viewed?
options: Falling blood pressure, signaled by tone pitch
Falling SpO2, signaled by the pulse tone pitch
A capnography alarm built into the pulse tone
An ECG rhythm change unrelated to saturation
questions.explanation: Pulse oximeter tone pitch tracks measured oxygen saturation, so a progressive fall in pitch alerts the provider to falling saturation without looking away from the patient or surgical field. The tone rate follows heart rate, but pitch does not encode blood pressure or capnography.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions most strongly promote alarm fatigue? (Select 2)
options: Difficulty localizing alarms in a noisy room
Turning alarm volumes to a clearly audible level
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue develops when clinicians hear frequent noncritical or false alarms and cannot easily tell which device is alarming in a noisy room, so they begin to tune out or silence alarms. Audible volumes, patient-specific limits, and variable-pitch oximeter tones reduce fatigue rather than cause it.

questions.stem: Which THREE consequences are typical of alarm fatigue? (Select 3)
options: Narrower alarm limits set by staff
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue leads clinicians to ignore, silence, or disable alarms, which delays recognition of true critical events and raises patient risk. Frequent noncritical alarms are a cause of alarm fatigue rather than a consequence, and staff experiencing it tend to widen limits rather than narrow them.

questions.stem: A healthy athlete has a baseline HR of 48 and repeatedly triggers a low-HR alarm set at 50. What is the best response?
options: Turn the low-HR alarm off since 48 is baseline
Keep the default limit and lower the volume
Individualize the limit within practice standards
Set the low-HR limit to 40 for every athlete
questions.explanation: Alarm limits can be adjusted to the patient's baseline, such as setting a low-HR limit just below 48 in a trained athlete, as long as the alarm stays on, audible, and within practice standards. Turning it off or muting it removes protection, and a blanket setting for every athlete ignores individual baselines.

questions.stem: SpO2 suddenly reads 86% with a noisy pleth waveform. Because prior alarms were artifact, the provider silences it without examining the patient or sensor. Which cognitive failure is MOST important?
options: Filtering nuisance alarms in a reasonable way
Not placing an arterial catheter for monitoring
Dismissing a valid alarm before verifying it
questions.explanation: Silencing an 86% reading without looking at the patient or sensor is anchoring on earlier false alarms, a premature-closure error, and a noisy pleth can coexist with true desaturation. The safe sequence is to check the patient's color, ventilation, and probe, then confirm the reading. Correct alarm limits and filtering are good practice, not the failure here.

questions.stem: A low-ETCO2 alarm sounds briefly during a previously stable anesthetic and then the value returns to baseline without intervention. What is the safest response?
options: Find the cause even though it self-corrected
Increase fresh gas flow and wait for a repeat
Assume artifact, since the value recovered
Change the threshold before checking the patient
questions.explanation: A brief low-ETCO2 alarm can reflect a partial disconnection, a sampling leak, a transient drop in cardiac output, or an embolic event, so the cause should be identified even when the number returns to baseline. Assuming artifact or moving the threshold first can miss an evolving problem.

questions.stem: A trainee says, 'The monitors will tell me if anything is wrong.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Technology by itself prevents most patient harm
Monitor data must be interpreted and acted on
Monitors reduce the need for clinical assessment
Alarms can replace a systematic room sweep
questions.explanation: Monitors only collect data; they cannot recognize context, artifact, or meaning, so harm is prevented when the provider watches trends, interprets them, and acts. Closed claims repeatedly show events in which monitors were present but their signals were missed or dismissed.

questions.stem: A stable anesthetic becomes unexpectedly hypotensive shortly after surgical positioning. The provider deliberately scans the patient, monitors, airway, machine, IVs, and surgical field in a fixed sequence. What is the principal advantage of this technique?
options: It replaces the need to answer single alarms
It proves the cause before treatment starts
It prevents omissions by forcing a full search
It satisfies the surgical time-out requirement
questions.explanation: A fixed sweep prevents attention from anchoring on a single abnormal number. Systematically scanning the patient, airway, monitors, machine, IVs, and field reduces omissions and can expose causes such as positioning, equipment, access, or surgical changes, while treatment of the hypotension proceeds in parallel.

questions.stem: Which THREE senses are explicitly part of proactive vigilance beyond monitor data? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Proactive vigilance uses sight, hearing, smell, and touch alongside the monitors: seeing chest movement and the field, hearing breath sounds and alarm tones, and smelling volatile agent or burning. Reviewing trends after the case is retrospective, and proprioception and taste are not used to monitor the patient.

questions.stem: During a machine sweep several hours into a case, which FOUR items should be checked? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: A periodic machine sweep checks that the vaporizer is delivering and has agent, that the ETCO2 water trap is not filling, that the absorbent has not changed color, and that the capnogram and its value make sense. The surgeon's tray and the room thermostat belong to other checks.

questions.stem: Which TWO patient-positioning checks belong in a routine anesthesia sweep? (Select 2)
options: Eyes taped and free from pressure
questions.explanation: The patient part of the sweep checks that the eyes are taped and free of pressure, the arms are secured without overextension, the head is midline, pressure points are padded, and lines are secure and functioning. Sponge and instrument counts and lighting belong to the surgical team.

questions.stem: Which FOUR surgical-field elements belong in the anesthesia sweep? (Select 4)
options: Blood loss in laps, suction, and floor
questions.explanation: The surgical field sweep tracks case status and upcoming critical points, blood loss in sponges, suction canisters, and on the floor, drape position, communication with the surgeon, and fire risk from lighted instruments and cautery. Closing technique and the next case's start time do not affect current anesthetic management.

questions.stem: During room preparation, suction and airway equipment are ready, but the workstation has not yet been checked. Using MS MAID, which setup element remains the first priority?
questions.explanation: MS MAID orders setup as Machine, Suction, Monitors, Airway, IV, and Drugs, and the machine check comes first because a faulty workstation can make every other preparation useless during induction. Ready suction and airway equipment do not replace the machine checkout.

questions.stem: Under MS MAID, what should be included in the 'Machine' check beyond the workstation itself?
options: The vaporizer level and ventilator settings
The CO2 absorbent and water trap
Full check plus a bag-mask and spare O2 cylinder
questions.explanation: The Machine step includes a complete workstation checkout plus a self-inflating bag-valve-mask and a full spare oxygen cylinder, so ventilation can continue if the machine or pipeline fails. Pipeline gauges, vaporizers, ventilator settings, absorbent, and water trap are parts of the full checkout rather than additions to it.

questions.stem: Immediately after induction, the patient regurgitates. A Yankauer is present but produces no suction because the canister valve was never opened. Which preinduction verification would have prevented this failure?
options: A Yankauer is physically present on the cart
Suction tested just for rapid sequence cases
The suction canister has been emptied of fluid
Suction assembled, on, working, and within reach
questions.explanation: Suction is ready only when the canister, tubing, and Yankauer are connected, the regulator is on, suction is confirmed at the tip, and it sits within reach of the head, because regurgitation can occur at any induction. A Yankauer on the cart or an empty canister does nothing if the system is not running.

questions.stem: Which FOUR airway items should be immediately available in the room under MS MAID? (Select 4)
options: Extra blade, handle, and ETT sizes
questions.explanation: MS MAID airway preparation includes a supraglottic airway, oral and nasal airways, a spare blade and handle, several tube sizes, a stylet, lubricant, and a cuff syringe so a failed first attempt can be followed at once. A flexible bronchoscope and chest tube tray are case-specific equipment rather than routine room setup.

questions.stem: During a routine ETT case, intubation fails and face-mask ventilation becomes inadequate. Which device already in the room is the first rescue for oxygenation?
questions.explanation: When intubation fails and face-mask ventilation is inadequate, the difficult airway algorithm moves to a supraglottic airway to restore oxygenation, so one should be in every room. A second blade, a bougie, or a fiberoptic scope are intubation aids that do not oxygenate a desaturating patient.

questions.stem: During a power failure, the laryngoscope light will not turn on. Which MS MAID preparation step was missed?
questions.explanation: MS MAID preparation includes checking that laryngoscope handles and other battery-powered devices work and that spare batteries are available, so a power failure does not disable airway equipment. A second suction source, spare blades, and drugs do not keep battery-powered devices running.

questions.stem: A patient enters the OR for general anesthesia and no monitors are attached yet. Which monitor is usually applied first?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry goes on first because it gives a baseline saturation and heart rate within seconds and guides preoxygenation, followed by blood pressure and the ECG with a baseline strip. Nasal cannula capnography is not part of the standard sequence before a general anesthetic induction.

questions.stem: A healthy patient has SpO2 100% after 30 seconds of preoxygenation, but expired oxygen is only 72%. Which finding BEST indicates that adequate denitrogenation has not yet occurred?
options: Expired O2 is below the target of about 90%
SpO2 has already reached 100% on the monitor
Inspired oxygen is reading 100% at the mask
Heart rate has not changed from baseline
questions.explanation: Denitrogenation is complete when expired oxygen reaches about 90%, which usually takes 3 to 5 minutes of tidal breathing or about 8 vital capacity breaths. SpO2 reaches 100% long before the FRC is filled with oxygen, and inspired oxygen shows only what is delivered, not what has replaced nitrogen in the lungs.

questions.stem: A patient cannot hold the mask during preoxygenation and both of your hands are needed elsewhere. What can maintain a reliable seal?
options: A loose mask with higher flow
An oral airway without a mask
questions.explanation: Mask head straps hold the seal while both hands are busy, so preoxygenation continues effectively; any leak entrains room air and slows denitrogenation. A loose mask with higher flow still leaks, and a nasal cannula alone gives a lower FiO2 than a sealed mask.

questions.stem: After LMA placement, chest excursion and bilateral breath sounds appear normal and SpO2 remains 100%. What additional finding is required to confirm ventilation through the device?
options: Stable pulse oximetry readings for 5 minutes
Sustained exhaled CO2 plus clinical assessment
A normal chest radiograph after placement
An unchanged blood pressure after placement
questions.explanation: ASA standards require that correct placement of an ETT or supraglottic airway be verified by clinical assessment and identification of exhaled CO2, because chest movement and breath sounds can mislead and SpO2 stays high after preoxygenation. A chest radiograph and blood pressure do not confirm ventilation through the device.

questions.stem: For an ETT or SGA, how long should continuous ETCO2 monitoring remain in use?
options: For the first 30 minutes after placement
From placement until removal or transfer
questions.explanation: ASA standards call for continual end-tidal CO2 monitoring from placement of an ETT or supraglottic airway until its removal or the start of transfer to postoperative care, because disconnection, dislodgement, and obstruction can occur at any point, including emergence. Monitoring stops only when the airway device is out or the patient is handed off.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, the capnogram suddenly disappears because the breathing circuit separates from the ventilator. Which required safety feature should independently alert the provider to this event?
options: A second capnograph on the expiratory limb
A processed EEG with a suppression alarm
An inline arterial blood gas analyzer
questions.explanation: When ventilation is controlled by a mechanical ventilator, ASA standards require a device that detects disconnection of breathing system components and gives an audible alarm, usually based on low airway pressure or low exhaled volume. A second capnograph, processed EEG, or blood gas analyzer is not required for this purpose.

questions.stem: During deep propofol sedation, a patient receives supplemental oxygen and maintains SpO2 99% while respiratory effort progressively decreases. Which monitoring combination is required to detect the problem before oxygen desaturation?
options: Clinical signs plus continuous exhaled CO2
Pulse oximetry with a 90% low-SpO2 alarm
Periodic arterial blood gases every 30 minutes
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen can keep SpO2 normal while propofol-related respiratory depression progresses. Continuous exhaled CO2 plus clinical observation detects decreasing ventilation earlier than waiting for hypoxemia, and intermittent checks miss changes between them.

questions.stem: During regional anesthesia with minimal or no sedation, what level of ventilation monitoring is required?
options: Arterial blood gases drawn at the start and every hour
Continual observation of qualitative clinical signs
questions.explanation: During regional anesthesia with no or minimal sedation, ASA standards require continual observation of qualitative clinical signs of ventilation, such as chest excursion and respiratory rate. Exhaled CO2 monitoring becomes expected once moderate or deep sedation is given, and blood gases or transcutaneous CO2 are not routine.

questions.stem: Which TWO bedside findings can support airway placement while capnography provides definitive confirmation? (Select 2)
options: A normal blood pressure after intubation
Smell of volatile at the patient's nose
questions.explanation: Condensation in the airway device and symmetric chest wall excursion support correct placement alongside breath sounds, while sustained capnography provides definitive confirmation. A stable SpO2 for one minute can persist after esophageal intubation because of preoxygenation, and blood pressure and absent stridor say nothing about tube position.

questions.stem: Why is a sustained capnogram over several consecutive breaths, rather than a single CO2 waveform, required to confirm tracheal intubation?
options: A single breath cannot display respiratory rate
Esophageal CO2 from gastric gas fades quickly
SpO2 must first fall to confirm intubation
The first breath is diluted by room air every time
questions.explanation: After mask ventilation or carbonated drinks, CO2 in the stomach can produce one or a few waveforms from an esophageal tube that shrink and disappear, so placement is confirmed only by a sustained capnogram over several consecutive breaths. SpO2 can stay normal for minutes after esophageal intubation, so it cannot be the confirming sign.

questions.stem: During a stable anesthetic, the provider notices a new sweet volatile odor near the workstation while every gas reading and alarm is still normal. Which principle of vigilance does this illustrate?
options: Odor confirms the vaporizer dial is accurate
Smell can confirm the tube is in the trachea
Odor is expected whenever low flows are used
Smell can reveal a leak before monitors change
questions.explanation: A new volatile odor near the workstation suggests a leak from a loose vaporizer filler cap, a cracked absorber canister, or a circuit connection, and smell can pick it up before inspired or expired agent values change. Low-flow anesthesia reduces rather than creates odor, and smell says nothing about tube position or dial accuracy.

questions.stem: Two hours into an uneventful anesthetic, every displayed value has remained stable. Which change in monitoring behavior is appropriate?
options: Reduce active surveillance and rely on alarms
None; vigilance remains continuous despite prolonged stability
Perform systematic sweeps only during induction and emergence
Delegate physiologic surveillance to the automated record
questions.explanation: Vigilance stays continuous throughout the anesthetic because stable periods are when attention drifts and events such as disconnections, drug errors, or bleeding go unnoticed. Automated records and alarms support surveillance but do not replace it, and systematic sweeps continue during maintenance, not just at induction and emergence.

questions.stem: A facility protocol permits NIBP cycling every 10 minutes during uncomplicated GA. What should the anesthesia provider do?
options: Use 10 minutes whenever ECG is continuous
Follow policy, since it overrides standards
questions.explanation: ASA and AANA standards set the minimum, requiring arterial pressure and heart rate evaluation at least every 5 minutes, and a facility policy cannot lower that floor. Continuous ECG does not substitute for pressure measurement, and waiting for instability means the first abnormal reading may come 10 minutes late.

questions.stem: A regional anesthetic is planned for a case that could become longer or more invasive than expected. What does keeping general anesthesia as backup to every plan require?
options: Airway gear kept outside until conversion is needed
General anesthesia induced before every block
Ready equipment and drugs for prompt conversion
Regional avoided whenever conversion is possible
questions.explanation: Any regional or MAC technique can fail or be outlasted by the surgery, so the drugs, airway equipment, and plan for general anesthesia must be ready in the room before starting. Keeping gear outside delays rescue, and avoiding regional or inducing GA first gives up the benefits of the regional technique.

questions.stem: Besides premedication and regional block drugs, which THREE drug categories belong in MS MAID preparation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: MS MAID drug preparation spans the anesthetic course: premedication, block drugs, induction and maintenance agents, reversal, emergency drugs, and medications for transport and PACU. Parenteral nutrition, home medications, and discharge prescriptions are managed by other teams and are not part of the anesthesia setup.

questions.stem: For a trauma laparotomy, which THREE elements belong in IV setup planning? (Select 3)
options: A fluid warmer and adequate IV size and number
questions.explanation: Trauma laparotomy needs planning for massive resuscitation: fluid type and tubing, pumps and a rapid infuser, a fluid warmer, and two or more large-bore lines. A single small IV and gravity drips cannot deliver blood fast enough, and hypotonic fluid is inappropriate for resuscitation.

questions.stem: Which set lists the standard monitors that should be ready before induction of a general anesthetic?
options: ECG, arterial line, SpO2, and processed EEG
NIBP, SpO2, and capnography without ECG
ECG, NIBP, SpO2, and cerebral oximetry
ECG, NIBP, SpO2, ETCO2, inspired/expired gases
questions.explanation: Standard setup for general anesthesia includes ECG, noninvasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, capnography, and inspired and expired gas analysis, with temperature and neuromuscular monitoring available as indicated. Arterial lines, processed EEG, and cerebral oximetry are added by indication rather than being standard.

questions.stem: During a seemingly stable anesthetic, the surgeon announces that major vascular clamping will occur in 2 minutes. Why is continuous awareness of surgical progress a monitoring skill rather than merely a workflow concern?
options: It lets the provider anticipate physiologic change
It lets anesthesia control the surgeon's pace
It mainly helps plan the next case start time
It replaces watching current physiologic trends
questions.explanation: Surgical events can abruptly change preload, afterload, blood loss, ventilation, or embolic risk. Knowing that vascular clamping is imminent lets the anesthesia provider prepare monitoring and treatment rather than reacting after deterioration occurs, while still watching current trends.

questions.stem: A new OR installs advanced automated monitors and assumes adverse events will decline without changing clinician workflow. Which limitation of monitoring technology is MOST important?
options: Automation removes most need for assessment
Data help only when clinicians interpret and act
Documentation quality decides whether harm is prevented
questions.explanation: Monitors and alarms prevent harm only when someone recognizes the signal, interprets it in context, and acts, so new technology without workflow change rarely reduces events. Alarm settings and documentation support that process but cannot replace active surveillance.

questions.stem: PIP rises from 20 to 35 cmH2O while plateau pressure remains 17 cmH2O and tidal volume is unchanged. Which mechanical change BEST explains the new pressure gradient?
options: Stiffer lungs with more elastic recoil
questions.explanation: Peak pressure includes both the resistive pressure needed to drive flow and the elastic pressure of the respiratory system, while plateau pressure, measured with no flow, reflects only the elastic part. A 15 cmH2O rise in PIP with an unchanged plateau and tidal volume means more resistive pressure from higher airway resistance, such as a kink, secretions, or bronchospasm.

questions.stem: Tidal volume is 500 mL, plateau pressure 25 cmH2O, and PEEP 5 cmH2O. What is static compliance?
questions.explanation: Static compliance = Vt / (Pplat - PEEP) = 500 / (25 - 5) = 25 mL/cmH2O. Forgetting to subtract PEEP gives 20 mL/cmH2O. Plateau pressure is used because it is measured without flow, so it excludes airway resistance.

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient has PIP 21 cmH2O and plateau pressure 19 cmH2O. What does the small pressure difference suggest?
options: Severe bronchospasm with otherwise normal compliance
Markedly reduced compliance of the respiratory system
A large leak in the breathing circuit lowering PIP
Little resistive pressure; airway resistance is normal
questions.explanation: The difference between peak and plateau pressure is the resistive component, so a gap of only 2 cmH2O means little pressure is being spent on airway resistance. Bronchospasm would widen the gap, reduced compliance would raise both pressures to higher levels, and a large leak would lower peak pressure and exhaled volume.

questions.stem: PIP and plateau pressure both increase by 10 cmH2O after steep Trendelenburg while tidal volume and inspiratory flow remain unchanged. Which mechanism is MOST likely?
options: Partial ETT obstruction from the head-down tilt
questions.explanation: Peak pressure reflects both resistive and elastic loads, whereas plateau pressure reflects alveolar pressure and respiratory-system compliance. A parallel rise in both after Trendelenburg, as abdominal contents push the diaphragm up, points to reduced compliance rather than an isolated increase in airway resistance.

questions.stem: PIP increases from 22 to 40 cmH2O while plateau remains 18 cmH2O after the patient's head is repositioned. Which problem should be investigated FIRST?
options: A larger tidal volume set on the ventilator
Increased resistance such as a kinked tube
questions.explanation: A rise in PIP from 22 to 40 with a stable plateau after moving the head points to added resistance in the tube, most often a kink, a bite, or the tip pushed against the carina, so the tube is checked first. A larger tidal volume, pneumoperitoneum, or pneumothorax would raise plateau pressure along with peak pressure.

questions.stem: A pressure trace shows PIP 38 and plateau 19 cmH2O. Which problem does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: Increased airway resistance, such as a kink or bronchospasm
Decreased lung compliance from abdominal insufflation
A larger tidal volume set on the ventilator
A circuit leak reducing the delivered volume
questions.explanation: A 19 cmH2O gap between peak and plateau pressure means extra pressure is being spent driving flow through the airways, so resistance has risen while compliance is unchanged. Kinks, secretions, biting, and bronchospasm fit, whereas insufflation or a larger tidal volume would raise plateau pressure too, and a leak would lower peak pressure.

questions.stem: A pressure trace shows PIP 36 and plateau 33 cmH2O. Which problem does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: Increased resistance from a kinked ETT
Decreased compliance, such as insufflation or pneumothorax
Secretions partially occluding the tube lumen during inspiration
questions.explanation: Peak 36 and plateau 33 cmH2O leave only a small resistive gap, so the high pressure comes from the elastic load, meaning compliance has fallen or tidal volume has increased. Insufflation, pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation, or a position change fit, whereas a kink, bronchospasm, or secretions would widen the gap between peak and plateau.

questions.stem: PIP rises abruptly from 22 to 38 cmH2O while plateau remains unchanged. Breath sounds are diminished but present bilaterally. Which bedside maneuver most directly distinguishes intraluminal ETT obstruction from other resistance causes?
options: Obtain a chest radiograph before manipulating the airway
Increase inspiratory flow and observe PIP
Pass a suction catheter through the ETT
questions.explanation: When peak pressure rises but plateau remains unchanged, the added pressure is occurring in the conducting airway rather than from reduced lung compliance. Passing a suction catheter directly tests tube patency and may identify secretions or a kink.

questions.stem: Which TWO problems raise PIP without significantly changing plateau pressure? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A kinked tube and bronchospasm increase airway resistance, so peak inspiratory pressure rises while plateau pressure, which reflects compliance at zero flow, stays nearly unchanged. Larger tidal volumes, pneumoperitoneum, pneumothorax, and Trendelenburg positioning reduce compliance or add volume and raise both peak and plateau pressures.

questions.stem: Which FOUR conditions can raise both PIP and plateau pressure? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Plateau pressure rises with anything that stiffens the respiratory system or increases the volume delivered, so insufflation, pneumothorax, steep Trendelenburg, and a larger tidal volume raise both peak and plateau. A kinked tube and higher inspiratory flow add resistive pressure and raise peak pressure alone.

questions.stem: A trainee interprets a pressure-volume loop as though pressure were on the vertical axis. Which correction is required before using loop slope to judge compliance?
options: Flow is vertical and volume is horizontal
Pressure is vertical and volume is horizontal
Flow is horizontal and pressure is vertical
Pressure is horizontal and volume is vertical
questions.explanation: On a pressure-volume loop, airway pressure is plotted on the horizontal axis and volume on the vertical axis, so a loop leaning toward the volume axis indicates higher compliance and one flattening toward the pressure axis indicates lower compliance. Reading the axes backward reverses that interpretation.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg, a pressure-volume loop shifts so that greater pressure is required to deliver the same volume. Which mechanical property has worsened?
questions.explanation: When the pressure-volume loop shifts so that more pressure is needed for the same volume, its slope flattens toward the pressure axis, meaning respiratory-system compliance has fallen, as expected with pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg. Airway resistance shows mainly as a wider loop and a peak-plateau gap, and dead space and oxygen extraction are not shown on the loop.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient develops prolonged expiration and a scooped expiratory limb on the flow-volume loop while plateau pressure remains unchanged. Which mechanical abnormality is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: A scooped, concave expiratory limb with prolonged expiration on the flow-volume loop shows reduced expiratory flow from narrowed airways, so airway resistance is increased, as in bronchospasm. An unchanged plateau pressure argues against reduced compliance, and dead space and oxygen consumption are not displayed on the loop.

questions.stem: Which FOUR conditions decrease respiratory compliance on a pressure-volume loop? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Reduced compliance means more pressure for the same volume, so the pressure-volume loop flattens toward the pressure axis. Pneumothorax, laparoscopic insufflation, inadequate muscle relaxation, and pulmonary edema all stiffen the lungs or chest wall. Emphysema increases compliance, and releasing insufflation restores it.

questions.stem: A patient with severe emphysema requires relatively little pressure to generate a given tidal volume compared with baseline. Which change in elastic mechanics does this represent?
options: Increased airway resistance with unchanged compliance
questions.explanation: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and elastic tissue, so the lungs distend with less pressure and the pressure-volume loop leans toward the volume axis, which is increased compliance. The same patients often have high airway resistance and air trapping, but that is a separate property from compliance.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum, the same 500-mL tidal volume requires substantially more pressure. How should the pressure-volume loop change?
options: It rotates toward the volume axis
It opens into a wide hysteresis
It flattens toward the pressure axis
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum pushes the diaphragm up and stiffens the respiratory system, so delivering the same 500 mL takes more pressure and the pressure-volume loop flattens toward the pressure axis. A loop rotating toward the volume axis would mean improved compliance, and wide hysteresis reflects resistance or recruitment rather than stiffness alone.

questions.stem: After the patient's head is turned, the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop flattens and PIP rises while plateau remains stable. Which mechanism BEST unifies these findings?
options: Larger tidal volume set on the ventilator
A disconnection at the circuit Y-piece
questions.explanation: Turning the head can kink the tube or push it against the carina, adding airway resistance, which raises PIP without changing plateau and slows expiratory flow, flattening the expiratory limb. Pneumoperitoneum or a larger tidal volume would raise plateau pressure, and a disconnection would lower pressures.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions primarily increase airway resistance rather than reduce compliance? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A kinked or obstructed tube and bronchospasm narrow the conducting airways, raising airway resistance and the peak-plateau gap. Raised abdominal pressure, pneumoperitoneum, pulmonary fibrosis, and morbid obesity stiffen the lungs or chest wall and lower compliance, raising plateau pressure as well.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has prolonged expiration, air trapping, high residual lung volume, and a scooped expiratory flow-volume limb. Which pattern BEST fits these findings?
options: Restrictive physiology with impaired inspiratory expansion
questions.explanation: Obstructive disease limits expiratory flow, so expiration is prolonged, air is trapped, residual volume rises, and the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop becomes scooped. Restrictive disease instead reduces volumes with a preserved shape, and a circuit disconnection would collapse the loop and pressures.

questions.stem: A patient has markedly reduced lung volumes but the basic contour of the flow-volume loop is preserved rather than scooped. Which pattern is MOST consistent?
questions.explanation: Restrictive physiology limits how far the lungs can expand, so volumes are small but flow relative to volume is preserved, giving a narrow loop with a normal contour. A scooped expiratory limb points to obstruction, variable intrathoracic obstruction flattens the expiratory limb, and a leak shows as an open loop that does not return to zero.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions produce a restrictive flow-volume pattern? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis stiffens the lungs and morbid obesity stiffens the chest wall and abdomen, so both reduce compliance and produce a restrictive flow-volume pattern with small volumes and a preserved shape. COPD, asthma, bronchospasm, and a kinked tube limit flow and produce an obstructive pattern.

questions.stem: During ventilation, the expiratory flow-volume limb begins flattening before the high-pressure alarm activates. What is the clinical advantage of recognizing this loop change?
options: It flags rising resistance before alarms trigger
It identifies the cause of any hypoxemia directly
It measures arterial oxygen tension directly
It replaces airway pressure alarm monitoring
questions.explanation: Real-time flow-volume and pressure-volume loops change shape as resistance or compliance changes, so a flattening expiratory limb can show a developing kink, secretions, or bronchospasm before pressure reaches the alarm threshold. Loops do not measure oxygenation or replace pressure alarms.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum, higher airway pressure is required to generate smaller tidal volumes and the pressure-volume loop shifts toward the pressure axis. Which pattern does this most closely mimic?
options: Obstructive mechanics from isolated airway resistance
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum pushes the diaphragm cephalad and stiffens the respiratory system, so higher pressure delivers a smaller volume and the pressure-volume loop flattens, mimicking restrictive mechanics. Obstructive mechanics would widen the peak-plateau gap and scoop the expiratory flow, a leak would leave the volume loop open, and rebreathing raises inspired CO2.

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects at the Y-piece. Which THREE alarms should be expected first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A Y-piece disconnection means the ventilator no longer meets resistance, so peak inspiratory pressure falls, no gas returns to the exhaled-volume sensor, and no CO2 reaches the sampling port. Those three low alarms together identify disconnection; high pressure or high PEEP alarms point to obstruction, and oxygen supply pressure is unaffected.

questions.stem: In volume-control ventilation, the high-pressure alarm sounds with every breath and exhaled tidal volume falls from 500 to 300 mL. Why has tidal volume fallen?
options: A circuit leak is losing part of each breath
Inspiration ends once the pressure limit is hit
The ventilator raised flow to compensate
Water in the flow sensor is reading low
questions.explanation: When peak pressure reaches the high-pressure limit, the ventilator stops inspiration early to protect the lungs, so the set tidal volume is not delivered and exhaled volume falls. The cause of the high pressure, such as a kink, bronchospasm, or reduced compliance, still has to be found. A leak would lower peak pressure rather than trigger the high-pressure alarm.

questions.stem: During volume-controlled ventilation, PIP, exhaled tidal volume, and ETCO2 all drift slightly downward together but remain above alarm thresholds. Which developing problem should be considered?
questions.explanation: A small leak lets part of each breath escape, so peak pressure, exhaled tidal volume, and ETCO2 drift down together before any threshold alarm sounds. Bronchospasm and pneumoperitoneum raise pressure, and a larger delivered volume would raise both pressure and exhaled volume.

questions.stem: Beyond disconnect detection, which FOUR ventilator alarms help identify dangerous circuit or patient conditions? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Besides disconnect detection, ventilator alarms include high peak pressure for obstruction or stiff lungs, sustained high airway pressure for a stuck valve or closed APL valve, negative pressure for a patient inspiring against a blocked circuit or active suction, and low oxygen supply pressure for pipeline failure. Volatile concentration and BIS alarms belong to other monitors.

questions.stem: During a routine ventilator sweep, which TWO parameter groups should be reviewed? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A ventilator sweep checks the mode, tidal volume and frequency, minute ventilation, peak, plateau, and mean airway pressures, PEEP, and loops for trends. Core temperature, suction volume, urine output, and vaporizer temperature are checked in other parts of the sweep.

questions.stem: Which THREE gases are routinely displayed as both inspired and expired concentrations? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Standard multigas monitors show inspired and expired concentrations of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, and the volatile agent, which lets the provider judge preoxygenation, rebreathing, and agent uptake. Carbon monoxide, helium, and argon are not routinely measured by the infrared and paramagnetic analyzers in anesthesia monitors.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation of a patient with severe COPD, the expiratory flow trace has not returned to zero when the next breath begins. What does this indicate?
options: A leak at the endotracheal tube cuff
questions.explanation: When expiratory flow has not reached zero before the next breath, the lungs have not finished emptying, so gas is trapped and intrinsic PEEP builds, raising intrathoracic pressure and risking hypotension and barotrauma. Lowering the rate or shortening inspiration lengthens expiratory time. A cuff leak shows as exhaled volume lower than delivered volume.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, PIP rises from 22 to 32 and plateau from 18 to 28. Which cause best fits this parallel increase?
options: A circuit leak at the Y-piece lowering delivered volume
questions.explanation: Pneumoperitoneum displaces the diaphragm cephalad and reduces respiratory-system compliance. Because the elastic load rises, both peak and plateau pressures increase together rather than producing the isolated peak-pressure rise expected from airway resistance.

questions.stem: PIP rises from 22 to 40 while plateau remains 18; suctioning retrieves thick secretions. Which mechanism caused the pressure change?
questions.explanation: Peak pressure rising by 18 cmH2O while plateau stays at 18 means the extra pressure is resistive, and thick secretions retrieved by suctioning confirm partial occlusion of the tube lumen. A pneumothorax or larger tidal volume would raise plateau pressure, and emphysema increases rather than decreases compliance.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, a previously paralyzed patient begins coughing against the ventilator and both peak and plateau pressures rise. Which cause BEST explains the transient fall in compliance?
options: Inadequate relaxation stiffening the chest wall
Emphysema raising compliance during the case
A new leak in the breathing circuit at the Y-piece
Pneumoperitoneum being released by the surgeon
questions.explanation: Coughing against the ventilator means active expiratory muscle effort and chest wall tension, which stiffens the respiratory system and raises both peak and plateau pressures until relaxation or depth is restored. A leak would lower pressures, and releasing pneumoperitoneum would improve compliance.

questions.stem: In ARDS, plateau pressure approaches 30 cmH2O while tidal volume is being adjusted. Why are continuous pressure-volume and flow-volume displays useful in addition to numeric alarms?
options: They replace capnography in patients with ARDS
They show overdistension or derecruitment early
They measure cardiac output breath by breath
They calculate arterial oxygen content each breath
questions.explanation: In ARDS, a pressure-volume loop that flattens at the top suggests overdistension, and changes in its lower portion suggest derecruitment, so loops can guide tidal volume and PEEP between numeric alarm thresholds. They do not measure cardiac output or oxygen content, and capnography is still required.

questions.stem: An oxygen analyzer has rapid response, no consumable electrochemical cell, and detects oxygen because of its attraction to a magnetic field. Which technology is being used?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic analyzers rely on oxygen's attraction to a magnetic field, measured as a pressure or displacement difference, which gives a fast response without a consumable cell. Galvanic and polarographic sensors use electrochemical cells that are consumed or need membranes, and infrared absorption is used for CO2 and volatile agents, not oxygen.

questions.stem: During maintenance, an oxygen analyzer becomes progressively sluggish after prolonged service because its sensing element is consumed by the measurement reaction. Which sensor type fits this failure mode?
questions.explanation: A galvanic fuel cell generates current from an oxygen-dependent chemical reaction that consumes its anode and electrolyte, so it slows and drifts with use and needs periodic replacement. Paramagnetic and infrared analyzers have no consumable sensing element, and mass spectrometry is a separate technology.

questions.stem: A polarographic Clark electrode is used for oxygen analysis. Which reaction occurs at the cathode?
questions.explanation: In a polarographic Clark electrode, a voltage is applied and oxygen diffusing across the membrane is reduced at the cathode, O2 + 2H2O + 4e- to 4OH-, so current is proportional to oxygen tension. The reverse reaction describes oxidation of water, and CO2 hydration describes the Severinghaus CO2 electrode.

questions.stem: During checkout, the oxygen sensor is found in the expiratory limb. Why should it instead sample the inspired limb?
options: To improve the accuracy of the capnography reading
To measure the patient's oxygen consumption directly
To catch hypoxic gas before it reaches the patient
To detect exhausted CO2 absorbent in the canister
questions.explanation: The inspired oxygen analyzer exists to catch a hypoxic mixture from pipeline crossover, flowmeter error, or an empty cylinder before the patient breathes it, so it must sample the inspiratory side. Expired oxygen is lower because of uptake and would delay or confuse that warning, and the analyzer has no role in capnography or absorbent assessment.

questions.stem: A removable galvanic oxygen sensor reads 18% while exposed to room air during checkout. What should occur before relying on it clinically?
options: Calibrate it to 50% oxygen from the flowmeter
Replace the vaporizer on that machine
Calibrate it with 100% oxygen by itself
Recalibrate it to read 21% oxygen first
questions.explanation: Galvanic sensors drift, so they are calibrated to room air at 21% oxygen daily and whenever the reading is off. A reading of 18% in room air means the sensor reads low and could mask or mimic a hypoxic mixture until it is recalibrated or replaced. The vaporizer has nothing to do with oxygen analysis.

questions.stem: Which response-time and accuracy specifications best match an acceptable oxygen analyzer?
options: Response in about 2–10 seconds with ±2% accuracy
questions.explanation: An acceptable inspired oxygen analyzer responds within roughly 2 to 10 seconds and is accurate to about plus or minus 2%, fast enough to warn of a hypoxic mixture within a few breaths. Responses of 30 seconds or longer would delay the warning, and sub-second response with 0.5% accuracy exceeds what standard analyzers provide.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, the oxygen pipeline remains normal but inspired O2 concentration gradually decreases. Which mechanism makes continuous inspired-O2 analysis essential?
options: Oxygen uptake can outpace replacement in the circuit
Low fresh gas flow directly causes oxygen toxicity
Low flow makes oxygen analyzers read falsely high
Nitrogen washout speeds up as fresh flow falls
questions.explanation: At low fresh gas flows, rebreathed circuit gas makes up much of the inspired mixture. Ongoing patient oxygen uptake can therefore lower circuit oxygen concentration despite a normal pipeline supply, which is why direct inspired oxygen measurement is essential.

questions.stem: FiO2 remains 0.50, but SpO2 falls to 84% after right mainstem intubation. What limitation of inspired-O2 monitoring does this illustrate?
options: Inspired O2 monitoring detects intubation errors
Adequate FiO2 does not guarantee arterial oxygenation
questions.explanation: The analyzer shows that 50% oxygen is being delivered, but a right mainstem intubation leaves the left lung perfused but unventilated, creating shunt, so SpO2 falls despite adequate FiO2. Inspired oxygen monitoring confirms delivery, not gas exchange, and it cannot detect tube position.

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects at the Y-piece. ETCO2 and exhaled tidal volume fall, but the inspired-O2 reading initially remains normal. Why?
options: Inspired O2 alarms are off while capnography runs
Fresh gas still flows past the inspiratory sensor
An O2 analyzer cannot detect any circuit problem
The sensor switches to room-air values when disconnected
questions.explanation: After a Y-piece disconnection, fresh gas keeps flowing through the inspiratory limb past the oxygen sensor, so FiO2 can read normally while the patient receives nothing. The disconnect shows first as low airway pressure, low exhaled volume, and loss of ETCO2, which is why those alarms, not the oxygen analyzer, detect it.

questions.stem: A galvanic oxygen sensor has a much shorter service life than expected despite correct calibration. Which repeated exposure can accelerate depletion of the cell?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with the alkaline electrolyte of a galvanic cell, so prolonged exposure, as when expired gas reaches the sensor, speeds depletion and shortens its life. Room air is used for calibration, and humidity and volatile agents have much less effect on the cell.

questions.stem: During airway laser surgery, SpO2 is adequate on FiO2 0.60. Before laser activation, which change most directly reduces oxidizer contribution to airway-fire risk?
options: Raise FiO2 to shorten the laser activation time
Raise fresh gas flow while keeping FiO2 0.60
Lower FiO2 to the minimum that keeps SpO2 safe
Replace oxygen with nitrous oxide at 60%
questions.explanation: During airway laser surgery, oxygen and nitrous oxide both support combustion, so FiO2 is reduced to the lowest level that maintains oxygenation, ideally 30% or less, with air as the balance. Higher flows at the same FiO2 do not reduce the oxidizer, and nitrous oxide is as dangerous as oxygen.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient has SpO2 99% despite suspected carbon monoxide exposure; another patient after topical benzocaine remains near SpO2 85% despite high FiO2. Which explanation BEST fits both findings?
options: CO pulls SpO2 toward 85%; MetHb reads falsely high
Anemia explains both readings about equally well
COHb reads as oxyhemoglobin; MetHb pulls toward 85%
questions.explanation: A two-wavelength pulse oximeter counts carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin because both absorb similarly at 660 nm, so SpO2 reads falsely high in CO poisoning. Methemoglobin absorbs at both wavelengths and drives the red-to-infrared ratio toward 1, which reads about 85%. Co-oximetry measures each species, and anemia alone does not shift SpO2.

questions.stem: An N2O-O2 proportioning system is working correctly. Which situation can still deliver a hypoxic mixture that only the inspired O2 analyzer would detect?
options: A pipeline crossover supplying the wrong gas
Turning N2O flow up while O2 stays low
Turning O2 flow down with N2O running
Setting N2O to 4 L/min and O2 to 1 L/min
questions.explanation: Proportioning systems link the N2O and O2 flow controls so the mixture stays at least about 25% oxygen, but they assume the oxygen pipeline actually carries oxygen. A crossover, a leak downstream of the flow controls, or a third gas can still deliver a hypoxic mixture, which only the inspired oxygen analyzer will catch. Raising N2O or lowering O2 on the flowmeters is exactly what the system prevents.

questions.stem: Which statement about clinical contraindications to inspired-O2 monitoring is correct?
options: It is contraindicated with nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: There are no clinical contraindications to inspired oxygen monitoring, because the analyzer samples gas in the breathing system rather than touching the patient, and it is required for every general anesthetic using a breathing system. COPD, pediatric age, and nitrous oxide use are reasons to watch FiO2 closely, not to omit it.

questions.stem: During stable general anesthesia, inspired O2 is 51% and expired O2 is 30%. What does this unusually wide gap suggest?
options: Normal oxygen uptake at this FiO2
High oxygen consumption or low ventilation
Excess fresh gas diluting expired gas
questions.explanation: The inspired-expired oxygen difference is normally about 4 to 6%, and it widens when oxygen consumption rises, as in hypermetabolic states, or when alveolar ventilation falls so each breath gives up more oxygen. A gap of 21% is far beyond normal uptake. High fresh gas flow narrows rather than widens the gap.

questions.stem: Which oxygen sensor measures current generated as O2 diffuses across a membrane and is reduced at an electrode?
questions.explanation: A polarographic Clark sensor applies an external voltage, and oxygen diffusing across its membrane is reduced at the cathode, producing a current proportional to oxygen tension. A galvanic cell generates its own current without an applied voltage, paramagnetic analyzers use magnetic attraction, and infrared absorption does not measure oxygen.

questions.stem: During machine checkout, the inspired-O2 analyzer displays the expected concentration but its low-concentration alarm is disabled. Which safety check remains incomplete?
options: The vaporizer fill level on the machine
The high-oxygen alarm limit setting by itself
Calibration and the low-O2 alarm function
The oxygen pipeline gauge pressure reading
questions.explanation: The daily checkout confirms that the oxygen analyzer is calibrated and that its low-concentration alarm is enabled with an appropriate limit, because the alarm is what warns of a hypoxic mixture. A correct reading with a disabled alarm leaves no warning if delivery fails while attention is elsewhere.

questions.stem: A gas analyzer identifies CO2, N2O, and volatile agents by wavelength-specific light absorption. Which technology is being used?
questions.explanation: Infrared analyzers pass light through the gas sample and measure absorption at wavelengths specific to CO2, N2O, and each volatile agent, which is how most sidestream monitors work. Oxygen and noble gases do not absorb infrared light, so oxygen is measured separately by paramagnetic or electrochemical cells.

questions.stem: At approximately which infrared wavelength does CO2 absorb strongly for capnographic measurement?
questions.explanation: Capnographs use infrared absorption, and CO2 absorbs strongly near 4.3 microns, so the drop in transmitted light at that wavelength reflects CO2 concentration. The 660 nm and 940 nm wavelengths are red and near-infrared light used by pulse oximeters, and 10 microns is outside the main CO2 absorption band.

questions.stem: During stable GA, PaCO2 is 41 mmHg and ETCO2 is 36 mmHg. In a healthy supine patient, how should this gradient be interpreted?
options: Reversed, because ETCO2 should normally exceed PaCO2
Abnormally wide, indicating major dead-space ventilation
Typical, because PaCO2 commonly exceeds ETCO2 by about 2–10 mmHg
questions.explanation: ETCO2 samples alveolar gas at end expiration, whereas PaCO2 reflects arterial blood after mixing from lung units with varying ventilation and perfusion. In a healthy patient, physiologic dead space usually leaves PaCO2 modestly higher than ETCO2.

questions.stem: Why will a standard infrared gas analyzer fail to measure xenon?
options: Xenon is too soluble to sample
Xenon absorbs infrared at CO2's wavelength
Xenon does not absorb infrared light
questions.explanation: Infrared analysis works only for molecules made of dissimilar atoms that absorb infrared energy, such as CO2, N2O, and volatile agents. Xenon is a single-atom noble gas with no infrared absorption, so it must be measured by other methods. If it absorbed at CO2's wavelength it would cause interference, not be invisible.

questions.stem: At the beginning of expiration, the capnogram remains at baseline before the rapid upstroke begins. What gas source dominates this initial exhaled volume?
options: Alveolar gas with the highest CO2 concentration
Fresh inspired gas entering the lungs
questions.explanation: At the start of exhalation, the gas leaving the airway comes from the trachea and conducting airways, which held fresh inspired gas and took no part in gas exchange, so CO2 stays at zero. The rapid upstroke begins when alveolar gas starts to mix in, and the plateau is mostly alveolar gas.

questions.stem: At what point on a normal time capnogram is ETCO2 measured?
options: At the end of the plateau, just before inspiration
At the beginning of the expiratory upstroke
At the midpoint of the flat alveolar plateau
At the bottom of the inspiratory downstroke
questions.explanation: ETCO2 is the CO2 value at the end of the alveolar plateau, just before inspiration starts, because that last-exhaled gas comes from alveoli and best approximates alveolar CO2. Earlier points include dead-space gas, and the downstroke reflects fresh inspired gas.

questions.stem: What physiologic event produces the rapid inspiratory downstroke on a normal capnogram?
options: Dead-space gas is exhaled before CO2 appears
Fresh CO2-free gas is inhaled past the sampler
Alveolar gas reaches a stable plateau
Rebreathed gas is inhaled with residual CO2
questions.explanation: The downstroke occurs when inspiration begins and fresh, CO2-free gas sweeps past the sampling site, so the reading drops quickly to zero. Dead-space exhalation is the flat start of phase I and the plateau is alveolar gas. Rebreathing would keep the baseline above zero rather than produce a clean fall to baseline.

questions.stem: Two patients have similar ETCO2 values, but one has a near-vertical expiratory upstroke while the other has a prolonged sloped upstroke. Which physiologic difference most directly explains the morphology?
options: The respiratory rate during the case
How evenly and quickly the alveoli empty
questions.explanation: The slope of the expiratory upstroke reflects how evenly alveoli empty; in normal lungs they empty together, giving a near-vertical rise, while obstructed units empty slowly and at different rates, stretching the rise into a slope. Cardiac output and respiratory rate change the ETCO2 value more than the upstroke shape.

questions.stem: A COPD patient has an alveolar plateau that continues to slope upward late in expiration instead of flattening. What produces this pattern?
options: Esophageal intubation with gastric CO2 washout
Uniform alveolar emptying across healthy lungs
Complete circuit disconnection at the Y-piece
Slow emptying of poorly ventilated, high-CO2 units
questions.explanation: In COPD, lung units with low ventilation relative to perfusion hold higher CO2 and empty last, so CO2 keeps rising through expiration and the plateau slopes upward. Uniform emptying gives a flat plateau, and esophageal intubation or disconnection produces fading or absent waveforms rather than a sloped plateau.

questions.stem: After intubation of an asthmatic patient, PIP increases, plateau pressure remains near baseline, and the capnogram develops a shark-fin contour. Which process BEST unifies these findings?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm narrows the airways, so peak pressure rises without much change in plateau, and alveoli empty slowly and unevenly, stretching the upstroke into a shark-fin shape. Restrictive disease raises plateau pressure, esophageal intubation gives fading or absent waveforms, and rebreathing raises the baseline.

questions.stem: Serial capnograms in a patient with bronchospasm show progressively greater rounding between the expiratory upstroke and alveolar plateau. What does this trend suggest?
options: Falling CO2 production from deeper anesthesia
More anatomic dead space without obstruction
Improving expiratory flow as spasm resolves
questions.explanation: Obstructed lung units empty slowly and at different rates, which prolongs the expiratory upstroke and slopes the plateau, so progressive rounding of the capnogram fits worsening airflow obstruction. Improving flow would make the upstroke steeper again, and dead space or CO2 production changes the value more than the shape.

questions.stem: A normally shaped capnogram shows progressively rising ETCO2. Which TWO mechanisms best explain this? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: When the capnogram keeps a normal shape but ETCO2 climbs, either less CO2 is being removed, from alveolar hypoventilation, or more is being produced, as with fever, sepsis, or a hypermetabolic state. Esophageal intubation, disconnection, cardiac arrest, and massive PE lower ETCO2 or abolish the waveform.

questions.stem: Which TWO events can transiently raise ETCO2 by washing accumulated CO2 back into circulation? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Releasing a tourniquet or an aortic cross-clamp returns blood that accumulated CO2 and acid in ischemic tissue, so ETCO2 rises transiently over a few minutes and ventilation may be increased to compensate. Hyperventilation and severe hypotension lower ETCO2, and esophageal intubation and disconnection abolish it.

questions.stem: A previously normal capnogram abruptly becomes flat immediately after the table is rotated. Which response is BEST?
options: Wait for SpO2 to fall to sort out the cause
Check airway, circuit, perfusion, and sampling now
Replace the CO2 absorbent before anything else
questions.explanation: A flat trace right after rotating the table can mean tube dislodgement, a circuit disconnection, a kinked sampling line, or a sudden fall in pulmonary blood flow, so each is checked immediately, starting with the patient and airway. Waiting for desaturation wastes the reserve capnography provides, and absorbent exhaustion raises rather than flattens the baseline.

questions.stem: After intubation, three sustained capnograms are present and bilateral breath sounds are heard. Which conclusion is justified by the CO2 finding alone?
options: It confirms the tube sits at midtracheal depth
It rules out a right mainstem intubation
It supports tracheal placement, not correct depth
It shows the tube is unlikely to move later
questions.explanation: Sustained exhaled CO2 shows the tube is ventilating the lungs rather than the esophagus, but a mainstem tube also produces CO2, so depth is checked separately by the lip mark, bilateral breath sounds, and cuff palpation or imaging. Tubes can also migrate with neck flexion or repositioning later.

questions.stem: During stable GA, FiO2, ETCO2, and end-tidal sevoflurane all fall abruptly at the same moment without a corresponding clinical change. Which explanation should be investigated first?
options: A shared gas-sampling or analyzer problem
questions.explanation: When oxygen, CO2, and volatile agent readings all change at the same moment without a clinical change, a shared component such as a cracked or disconnected sampling line, a full water trap, or the analyzer itself is the likely cause. Physiologic events usually change one gas, such as CO2 with a fall in pulmonary blood flow.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after CO2 insufflation for laparoscopy, ETCO2 has risen from 35 to 52 mmHg and crepitus is felt over the chest wall. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Peritoneal absorption normally raises ETCO2 modestly after insufflation, but a continuing large rise with crepitus over the chest wall means CO2 is tracking into subcutaneous tissue, which absorbs it over a large surface. Exhausted absorbent would raise the inspired baseline, and sepsis would not cause crepitus.

questions.stem: Which THREE conditions widen the PaCO2–ETCO2 gradient by increasing alveolar dead space? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Alveolar dead space is lung that is ventilated but poorly perfused, so CO2 from those units never reaches the exhaled gas and ETCO2 falls further below PaCO2. Embolism and low cardiac output reduce perfusion, and emphysema destroys capillary beds. Hyperventilation and fever change both values in the same direction without widening the gap, and rebreathing raises inspired and arterial CO2 rather than dead space.

questions.stem: A small child is connected to equipment that adds excessive apparatus dead space. PaCO2 rises while sampled ETCO2 underestimates the arterial value. Which mechanism contributes to the discrepancy?
options: Faster sidestream sampling from smaller airways
A bigger wasted fraction diluting alveolar gas
Higher pediatric CO2 production on its own
Lower circuit resistance in small children
questions.explanation: Adult connectors, filters, and elbows add apparatus dead space that is large relative to a child's small tidal volume, so a bigger share of each breath is dead-space gas, PaCO2 rises from rebreathing, and the sampled end-tidal gas is diluted. Pediatric equipment with minimal dead space restores agreement.

questions.stem: A premature infant has extremely low minute ventilation. Why can a conventional sidestream capnograph itself become clinically significant?
options: It samples too little gas to detect neonatal CO2
The line adds resistance without removing gas
Sampling removes much of the infant's ventilation
Sidestream monitoring raises the infant's FiO2
questions.explanation: Sidestream analyzers aspirate roughly 50 to 250 mL/min, which can be a large fraction of a premature infant's minute ventilation, reducing delivered ventilation and diluting the sample with fresh gas so ETCO2 reads low. Low-flow or mainstream analyzers avoid the problem.

questions.stem: A 900-g infant receives 40 mL tidal volumes at 6 breaths/min while a sidestream analyzer removes 150 mL/min. Approximately what fraction of the calculated 240 mL/min minute ventilation is being sampled?
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation is 6 × 40 = 240 mL/min, and 150 / 240 is about 0.6, so the analyzer removes about 60% of each minute's ventilation. In very small infants this distorts the waveform, lowers delivered tidal volume, and dilutes readings, so low-flow sampling or mainstream capnography is preferred.

questions.stem: Condensation repeatedly occludes a sidestream sampling line. Which simple positioning change reduces water entry?
options: Lower the sampling line below the circuit
Keep the sampling port pointing up
questions.explanation: Condensed water runs downhill, so keeping the sampling port pointing upward on the circuit lets water drain away from the line instead of into it, and the water trap or hydrophobic filter catches the rest. Raising the sampling rate or placing the line below the circuit pulls in more water, and turning off humidification sacrifices airway humidity.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, the capnogram inspiratory baseline rises to 6 mmHg and no longer returns to zero. Which abnormality is demonstrated regardless of its cause?
questions.explanation: An inspiratory baseline above zero means CO2 is present in inspired gas, so the patient is rebreathing exhaled gas, whatever the cause. Exhausted absorbent, a sticking unidirectional valve, or fresh gas flow too low for the circuit are the usual sources. Disconnection or esophageal intubation flatten the trace instead.

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 is elevated. Which THREE circuit causes should be checked first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Inspired CO2 in a circle system comes from exhausted absorbent, an incompetent inspiratory or expiratory unidirectional valve, or fresh gas flow too low for the circuit, so those are checked first. Bronchospasm changes waveform shape, esophageal intubation removes the waveform, and pulmonary embolism lowers ETCO2 without raising the baseline.

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 remains above zero on low fresh-gas flow. Which cause best fits this rebreathing pattern?
options: Exhausted CO2 absorbent or a sticking valve
