Convection to moving air is second, while conduction to the table and evaporation from wounds and airways contribute less in most cases.

questions.stem: During an open abdominal case, approximately 200 g of water evaporates from exposed tissue. Using about 0.58 kcal lost per gram evaporated, what heat loss is attributable to evaporation?
questions.explanation: Evaporative heat loss is mass times latent heat: 200 g x 0.58 kcal/g = 116 kcal. Using half the latent heat gives 58 kcal, and counting grams as kilocalories gives 200. Large open cavities and dry gases make evaporation a meaningful share of heat loss.

questions.stem: Which FOUR sites are appropriate core-temperature measurement locations? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The distal esophagus, bladder, pulmonary artery, and nasopharynx reflect core temperature well, as do the tympanic membrane and rectum, although rectal and bladder readings lag during rapid change. Forehead strips and axillary readings are peripheral and underestimate core temperature.

questions.stem: Core temperature is 36.0 °C and mean skin temperature is 32.0 °C. Using mean body temperature ≈ 0.85(core) + 0.15(skin), what is the approximate value?
questions.explanation: Mean body temperature = 0.85 x 36 + 0.15 x 32 = 30.6 + 4.8 = 35.4 C. Using core temperature alone overstates total heat content, and an equal-weight average (34 C) understates it, because core tissues hold most of the body's heat.

questions.stem: During rapid active rewarming, pulmonary-artery temperature rises promptly but rectal temperature changes slowly. How should the discrepancy be interpreted?
options: The rectal probe has likely malfunctioned
Rectal temperature can lag core changes
Rectal readings lead PA readings in warming
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature lags true core temperature during rapid change because the rectum has low blood flow and its contents act as a heat sink, while pulmonary artery blood reflects central temperature almost at once. A gap during rewarming is expected and does not mean either probe has failed.

questions.stem: Distal esophageal temperature is 36.5 °C while skin temperature is 33 °C. Which statement best describes whole-body thermal status?
options: Skin temperature best represents total heat content
Esophageal temperature equals mean body temperature
Neither equals mean body temperature; core weighs more
Core and skin should be averaged with equal weight
questions.explanation: Mean body temperature weights core about 0.85 and skin about 0.15, so here it is about 0.85 x 36.5 + 0.15 x 33, roughly 36 C, below the esophageal reading but far above the skin value. Neither site alone describes whole-body heat content.

questions.stem: During volatile anesthesia, ETCO2 rises rapidly despite increased minute ventilation and heart rate climbs to 130/min, but core temperature is only 37.2 °C. Which interpretation is safest?
options: A normal temperature effectively rules out MH
Rising ETCO2 argues against MH in this case
MH usually begins with fever before hypercarbia
MH remains possible; fever is a late sign
questions.explanation: In malignant hyperthermia, hypermetabolism raises CO2 production first, so a rising ETCO2 despite increased ventilation and unexplained tachycardia are early signs, while temperature may rise only later. A normal temperature does not exclude it, and the volatile agent should be stopped and dantrolene prepared if the picture fits.

questions.stem: At the end of a 6-hour case, core temperature is 34.9 °C. Which FOUR complications should be anticipated? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia increases oxygen consumption through shivering, impairs platelets and clotting enzymes, raises wound infection risk, and slows drug metabolism. It therefore delays rather than speeds emergence and prolongs neuromuscular blockade.

questions.stem: A lightly sedated, awake patient undergoes a 30-minute hand procedure under regional anesthesia and maintains normal thermoregulatory responses. Why may continuous core-temperature monitoring add little in this specific setting?
options: Skin temperature suffices during any sedation
Short case; the patient can shiver and constrict
Temperature monitoring is unsafe with regional
Temperature never matters in awake patients
questions.explanation: An awake patient with intact thermoregulation can shiver and vasoconstrict, and a 30-minute hand case rarely produces a meaningful change, so continuous core monitoring adds little unless the case extends or sedation deepens. Temperature still matters in awake patients during longer neuraxial cases, where thermoregulation is impaired.

questions.stem: During cardiac surgery, temperature can be read from a bladder catheter, a thermodilution catheter, a forehead strip, or an axillary probe. Which gives the best direct core estimate?
questions.explanation: Blood in the pulmonary artery is mixed central venous blood, so a thermistor there gives the reference standard for core temperature and responds quickly during cooling and rewarming. Forehead strips, axillary probes, and skin sites are peripheral and read lower than core.

questions.stem: Both a patient under general anesthesia and one under neuraxial anesthesia develop perioperative hypothermia. Which shared mechanism contributes?
options: Both impair thermoregulatory control and vasoconstriction
Both raise the vasoconstriction threshold above normal
Neuraxial block raises central heat production
questions.explanation: General anesthesia lowers the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds centrally, and neuraxial anesthesia blocks sympathetic vasoconstriction and shivering below the block and lowers thresholds by reducing afferent input, so both allow redistribution of core heat to the periphery. Neither raises the vasoconstriction threshold or increases heat production.

questions.stem: Heat is lost to cool walls, the operating table, and moving air. Which THREE mechanisms are involved? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Heat is lost to cool walls by radiation, to the table by conduction, and to moving air by convection. Evaporation from wounds and airways is a fourth mechanism but not the one described for walls, table, and air, and diffusion and osmosis are mass-transfer processes.

questions.stem: During active rewarming after cardiopulmonary bypass, nasopharyngeal and rectal temperatures differ substantially. Why can monitoring more than one site be useful?
options: Rectal temperature changes first during rewarming
Sites equilibrate at different rates when changing
Core sites should match closely throughout
PA temperature lags peripheral sites when warming
questions.explanation: During rapid cooling or rewarming, well-perfused sites such as the nasopharynx and pulmonary artery change quickly, while bladder and rectal readings lag, so monitoring two sites shows both how fast the core is changing and whether the whole body has caught up. A large gap after bypass warns of afterdrop once warming stops.

questions.stem: A short anesthetic is expected to cause little thermal disturbance, whereas another case involves deliberate cooling and rewarming. Which principle determines the need for temperature monitoring?
options: Monitor pediatric patients and no one else
Monitor during cardiac surgery and nowhere else
Monitor when significant change is expected
Begin monitoring after MH becomes suspected
questions.explanation: ASA standards call for temperature monitoring whenever clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected, which covers deliberate cooling, long or open cases, and suspected hyperthermia regardless of age or surgical specialty. Waiting until malignant hyperthermia is suspected would miss the early trend.

questions.stem: During laparoscopic hiatal hernia repair, peak and plateau pressures rise, SpO2 falls to 88%, BP drops to 75/40, and left breath sounds diminish. What is the most likely cause?
options: Right mainstem intubation from tube migration
Tension capnothorax from a pleural tear
questions.explanation: During hiatal dissection, CO2 can enter the pleural space through a tear, and rising peak and plateau pressures with falling SpO2, hypotension, and unilateral loss of breath sounds signal tension capnothorax. Mainstem intubation raises pressures and lowers SpO2 but rarely causes hypotension, bronchospasm keeps the plateau normal, and simple absorption raises ETCO2 without circulatory collapse.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes after CO2 insufflation, ETCO2 has risen gradually from 35 to 45 mmHg with a normal waveform, zero baseline, and stable airway pressures. What is the best response?
options: Increase minute ventilation to clear absorbed CO2
Ask the surgeon to release pneumoperitoneum now
Change the absorbent, which must be exhausted
Give bicarbonate to buffer the rising CO2
questions.explanation: A gradual 10 mmHg rise after insufflation with a zero baseline and normal waveform is expected absorption of CO2 from the peritoneum, and increasing rate or tidal volume clears it. Releasing pneumoperitoneum is reserved for complications such as capnothorax or embolism, exhausted absorbent would raise the inspired baseline, and bicarbonate generates more CO2.

questions.stem: During spontaneous ventilation through a circle system, a negative-pressure alarm sounds with each inspiration and the reservoir bag collapses. What is the most likely cause?
options: An APL valve closed during spontaneous breaths
Fresh gas flow below minute ventilation
A leak at the Y-piece letting in room air
Exhausted CO2 absorbent in the canister
questions.explanation: During spontaneous breathing, the patient inspires from the reservoir bag, so if fresh gas flow is less than minute ventilation the bag empties and inspiration pulls negative pressure in the circuit; an active scavenger drawing through a faulty interface can do the same. A closed APL valve causes high, not negative, pressure, and a leak lets room air in rather than creating suction.

questions.stem: A small cuff leak develops before any alarm threshold is crossed. Which THREE subtle trends may appear first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A small cuff leak lets part of each breath escape, so peak pressure falls slightly, exhaled volume drops below the set volume, and ETCO2 dips as exhaled gas is lost and diluted, all before alarm thresholds are crossed. A leak does not raise plateau pressure, add inspired CO2, or cause a curare cleft.

questions.stem: With fresh absorbent in place, the capnogram's inspiratory downstroke becomes slanted and the baseline no longer returns to zero. Which component is most likely faulty?
options: Exhausted CO2 absorbent in the canister
A leaking APL valve venting fresh gas
questions.explanation: When the inspiratory unidirectional valve does not seal, exhaled gas flows back into the inspiratory limb during expiration and is rebreathed at the start of the next breath, so the downstroke slants and the inspired baseline rises even with fresh absorbent. Absorbent exhaustion is excluded here, a leaking APL valve lowers circuit pressure rather than adding CO2, and an obstructed line damps the whole waveform.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has PaCO2 50 mmHg and mixed expired CO2 25 mmHg. Using the Bohr-Enghoff equation, what is the dead space fraction (VD/VT)?
questions.explanation: VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2 = (50 - 25) / 50 = 0.5, meaning half of each breath is dead space, well above the normal 0.2 to 0.3. Dividing by PECO2 instead gives 1.0. A high dead space fraction is why ETCO2 underestimates PaCO2 in COPD, embolism, and low-output states.

questions.stem: During hip arthroplasty, BP falls to 70/40, SpO2 drops to 86%, and ETCO2 abruptly falls just as the femoral canal is pressurized with PMMA and the stem seated. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Hypotension, hypoxemia, and an abrupt ETCO2 fall at the moment of cementing and prosthesis insertion are the classic picture of bone cement implantation syndrome, caused by marrow fat, cement particles, and air embolizing to the lungs and raising pulmonary vascular resistance. Anaphylaxis would bring rash and bronchospasm, bleeding produces gradual hypotension, and hypoventilation raises ETCO2.

questions.stem: The sidestream sampling line cracks near the monitor, but the patient's ventilation is unchanged. What happens to the displayed gas values?
options: CO2 reads high from room air entering the line
Readings stay accurate because pump flow is constant
CO2 and agent read low as room air dilutes them
FiO2 reads 100% from gas trapped in the line
questions.explanation: A crack lets the pump draw room air along with the sample, so CO2 and agent readings fall and inspired oxygen drifts toward 21% while the patient's actual gases are unchanged. Room air contains almost no CO2, so it cannot raise the reading. Checking the line before treating the numbers prevents chasing an artifact.

questions.stem: During stable ventilation, ETCO2 alone rises from 38 to 55 mmHg while FiO2 and measured anesthetic-agent concentrations remain stable. Which category should be investigated first?
questions.explanation: When only ETCO2 rises while oxygen and agent readings stay stable, the analyzer and sampling line are working, so the cause lies with the patient or ventilation: hypoventilation, increased CO2 production as in fever or a hypermetabolic state, absorption of insufflated CO2, or rebreathing. A shared analyzer problem would change all gases together.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, a notch appears in every alveolar plateau and the surgeon reports increasing abdominal tone long after the last rocuronium dose. What should be assessed next?
options: CO2 absorbent exhaustion with rebreathing gas
Quantitative NM monitoring and relaxation needs
questions.explanation: A notch in each plateau with rising abdominal tone long after the last rocuronium dose means neuromuscular blockade is wearing off and the diaphragm is contracting, so quantitative monitoring guides whether to redose or deepen anesthesia. Bronchospasm, rebreathing, and sampling obstruction change the waveform differently and would not explain increasing muscle tone.

questions.stem: During CPR with a confirmed tracheal tube, ETCO2 stays at 7 mmHg. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Compressions are generating too little flow
The ventilation rate during CPR is too slow
The sampling line is reading falsely high
questions.explanation: During CPR with a confirmed tracheal tube, ETCO2 reflects the pulmonary blood flow that compressions generate, so a value below about 10 mmHg signals poor compression quality and prompts a change in rate, depth, or compressor. Return of circulation raises ETCO2 abruptly, and slower ventilation tends to raise rather than lower it.

questions.stem: At sea level, FiO2 is 0.50, PaCO2 is 40 mmHg, and PaO2 is 55 mmHg. What is the approximate A-a oxygen gradient?
questions.explanation: PAO2 = 0.50 x (760 - 47) - 40/0.8 = 356 - 50 = 306 mmHg, so the A-a gradient is 306 - 55, about 250 mmHg, which points to shunt or V/Q mismatch rather than a delivery failure. Using room-air FiO2 gives about 45, omitting water vapor pressure gives about 275, and stopping at PAO2 gives about 307.

questions.stem: Oxygen pipeline pressure suddenly falls during a nitrous oxide and oxygen anesthetic. Which machine component shuts off or reduces nitrous oxide flow?
options: Oxygen flush valve at the common outlet
questions.explanation: The fail-safe valve senses oxygen supply pressure and shuts off or proportionally reduces nitrous oxide when it falls, with a low-pressure alarm. It responds to pressure, not concentration, so it cannot stop a hypoxic mixture if the pipeline carries the wrong gas. The proportioning system links flowmeter settings, and the flush bypasses the flowmeters.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, inspired O2 falls from 50% to 32% despite unchanged flowmeter settings and no pipeline problem. Which mechanism should be considered?
options: Analyzers cannot work at low fresh gas flow
The absorbent consumes oxygen in the canister
Oxygen uptake is a large share of low fresh flow
questions.explanation: At low fresh gas flows, a patient consuming about 250 mL/min of oxygen removes a large share of the oxygen delivered, and nitrogen or nitrous oxide accumulates in the circle, so inspired oxygen falls even with unchanged flowmeters. Raising oxygen flow corrects it. Vaporizers and absorbent do not consume oxygen.

questions.stem: During pediatric airway laser surgery, a flame appears in the tracheal tube. What should be done first?
options: Remove the tube and stop all airway gases
Leave the tube in and flush it with saline
Finish the laser step, then assess the airway
questions.explanation: For an airway fire, ASA guidance is to remove the tracheal tube and stop the flow of all airway gases at once, pour saline into the airway, then ventilate by mask with low oxygen once the fire is out and inspect the airway with bronchoscopy. Leaving a burning tube in place or continuing oxygen feeds the fire.

questions.stem: A confused patient from an enclosed-space fire has a COHb of 25%. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
options: Sodium nitrite to bind carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: High-flow 100% oxygen shortens carboxyhemoglobin half-life from about 4 to 5 hours on room air to roughly 60 to 90 minutes, and hyperbaric oxygen shortens it further in severe cases. Titrating to SpO2 is meaningless because the oximeter reads COHb as oxyhemoglobin, and methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia, not CO poisoning.

questions.stem: After topical benzocaine, SpO2 settles near 85% and changes little with 100% oxygen. Which diagnosis best explains this saturation behavior?
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin absorbs red and infrared light about equally, driving the oximeter ratio toward 1, which displays as about 85%, and the reading changes little with added oxygen because the problem is the hemoglobin, not the oxygen supply. Benzocaine is a classic trigger. Hypoventilation would improve with oxygen, and CO poisoning reads falsely high.

questions.stem: During pediatric anesthesia, SpO2 falls after marked head flexion while a persistent ETCO2 waveform remains. Breath sounds are now asymmetric. Which airway problem is most likely?
questions.explanation: Neck flexion pushes the tube tip deeper, and in a child's short trachea it easily enters a mainstem bronchus, causing desaturation from shunt and asymmetric breath sounds while CO2 is still exhaled from the ventilated lung. Esophageal displacement or disconnection would lose the waveform, and bronchospasm causes bilateral wheezing.

questions.stem: A cold, vasoconstricted patient has an intermittent SpO2 signal while the ECG rate remains stable. What is the best first step to improve measurement reliability?
options: Warm the hand or move the probe to a better site
Assume hypoxemia and intubate the patient at once
Raise FiO2 until the pleth waveform comes back
Use ETCO2 in place of oxygenation monitoring
questions.explanation: A stable ECG rate with an intermittent pleth in a cold patient points to poor peripheral perfusion, not hypoxemia, so warming the extremity or moving the sensor to the ear, nose, or forehead restores the signal. Raising FiO2 does not create pulsatile flow, and ETCO2 measures ventilation, not oxygenation.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation at 8 mL/kg in sinus rhythm with a closed chest, arterial pulse pressure variation is 18%. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The patient is likely volume overloaded
The patient is likely fluid responsive
The arterial line is underdamped and ringing
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure variation above about 12 to 13% during controlled ventilation with tidal volumes of at least 8 mL/kg, a closed chest, and sinus rhythm suggests the heart is on the steep part of the Starling curve, so a fluid bolus will likely raise stroke volume. Volume overload gives low variation, and the index is unreliable with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmias, or small tidal volumes.

questions.stem: During MAC with nasal capnography, the ETCO2 waveform disappears while the patient remains awake, talking, and clinically well ventilated. What should be checked first?
options: Apnea, even though the patient is still talking
Complete airway obstruction needing treatment now
Sampling position and mouth breathing past the cannula
questions.explanation: A patient who is awake and talking is moving air, so a lost nasal capnogram most likely reflects a displaced cannula, a blocked line, or exhaled gas leaving through the mouth instead of the nares. Repositioning the sampler or using an oral-nasal cannula restores the trace. Apnea or complete obstruction is not compatible with conversation.

questions.stem: PIP abruptly rises from 20 to 45 cmH2O, plateau pressure is unchanged, and wheezing is present. Which response best addresses the likely mechanical problem?
options: Reduce FiO2, since oxygen raised the pressure
Increase tidal volume to push past resistance
Increase PEEP since lung compliance has fallen
Check tube and circuit while treating bronchospasm
questions.explanation: Peak pressure includes resistive plus elastic pressure, while plateau pressure reflects the elastic load. A sharp rise in peak pressure with an unchanged plateau and wheezing localizes the problem to airway resistance, so tube or circuit obstruction and bronchospasm are the immediate targets. Compliance has not fallen, and larger breaths raise pressure further.

questions.stem: At the end of surgery, train-of-four at the orbicularis oculi shows 4 twitches without fade, but the adductor pollicis shows 2 twitches. Which reading should guide reversal and extubation?
options: The thumb reading via the ulnar nerve
The eye muscle reading near the brow
The average of the two sites
questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi recovers sooner than peripheral muscles, and stimulation near the eye can directly activate muscle, so it overestimates readiness for extubation. The adductor pollicis, stimulated through the ulnar nerve, reflects recovery of the upper airway muscles more closely and is the standard site for confirming a TOF ratio of 0.9.

questions.stem: A pressure-volume loop no longer closes because measured expiratory volume is consistently less than inspiratory volume. Which problem should be investigated?
questions.explanation: When exhaled volume is consistently less than inspired volume, the pressure-volume loop does not return to its starting point, which means gas is escaping through a cuff or circuit leak. Bronchospasm and compliance changes alter the loop's slope or width but still let it close.

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient with unilateral vocal cord paralysis has a flow-volume loop with a flattened inspiratory limb and a normal expiratory limb. Which pattern is this?
questions.explanation: During forced inspiration, negative airway pressure collapses an extrathoracic lesion such as a paralyzed vocal cord, so the inspiratory limb flattens while expiratory flow, which pushes the lesion open, stays normal. A variable intrathoracic lesion flattens the expiratory limb instead, and a fixed obstruction flattens both limbs.

questions.stem: A morbidly obese patient requires high peak and plateau pressures to deliver relatively small tidal volumes, without a large peak-to-plateau gradient. Which pattern best fits?
options: Normal respiratory mechanics for body size
A major leak in the breathing circuit
questions.explanation: High peak and plateau pressures with only a small gap between them mean the extra pressure is elastic, from a stiff chest wall and abdomen pushing on the diaphragm, which is a restrictive pattern. Airway obstruction would widen the peak-plateau gap, and a leak lowers pressures.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, pneumoperitoneum reduces compliance and ETCO2 gradually rises despite unchanged ventilation. Which adjustment most directly addresses the CO2 trend while lung mechanics are reassessed?
options: Lower minute ventilation to cut airway pressure
Increase FiO2 and leave the ventilation unchanged
Raise minute ventilation within protective pressures
questions.explanation: Absorbed CO2 from the peritoneum raises the CO2 load, so minute ventilation is increased, usually by raising the rate while keeping plateau pressure within protective limits and using PEEP or recruitment for the reduced compliance. Lowering ventilation worsens hypercapnia, and FiO2 does not affect CO2 removal.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly falls to zero, but PIP and exhaled tidal volume remain unchanged and hemodynamics are stable. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Massive pulmonary embolism with cardiovascular collapse
questions.explanation: When peak pressure and exhaled volume are unchanged and hemodynamics are stable, the patient is still being ventilated and perfused, so a sudden zero ETCO2 points to the sampling line being disconnected, kinked, or blocked. A circuit disconnection would drop pressure and volume, and arrest or massive embolism would change hemodynamics.

questions.stem: During positive-pressure ventilation through a first-generation LMA, peak pressure reaches 28 cmH2O, an audible leak develops, and gurgling is heard over the epigastrium. What is the most likely problem?
options: Airway pressure is above the cuff's seal
questions.explanation: First-generation LMAs typically seal at about 20 cmH2O, so a peak pressure of 28 forces gas past the cuff into the pharynx and esophagus, causing an audible leak, lost tidal volume, and gastric insufflation that raises aspiration risk. Lowering peak pressure, deepening anesthesia, or switching to a second-generation device or a tube fixes it. Bronchospasm would not push gas into the stomach.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, the capnogram becomes flat and the patient is visibly apneic although SpO2 remains 99% on supplemental oxygen. What is the immediate priority?
options: Open the airway and support ventilation
Raise oxygen flow and recheck the SpO2
Replace the sampling line, then reassess
questions.explanation: A flat capnogram with visible apnea is apnea whatever the SpO2, because supplemental oxygen delays desaturation by minutes. The airway is opened and ventilation supported at once while sedation is reduced. Raising oxygen flow or changing the sampling line first wastes the early warning that capnography gives.

questions.stem: ETCO2 transiently rises immediately after IV sodium bicarbonate despite unchanged ventilation. Which mechanism best explains the change?
options: A sudden rise in metabolic rate from fever
Rebreathing from a sticking expiratory valve
Buffering makes CO2 that the lungs must clear
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate combines with hydrogen ions to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into water and CO2, so a bolus produces a transient rise in PaCO2 and ETCO2 until the lungs clear it. With fixed ventilation the rise appears within a minute or two and fades. Malignant hyperthermia causes a sustained rise with tachycardia.

questions.stem: During one-lung ventilation, ETCO2 is 25 mmHg while simultaneous PaCO2 is 55 mmHg. Which mechanism best explains the widened gradient?
options: A normal fixed gradient during one-lung ventilation
Increased V/Q mismatch and alveolar dead space
questions.explanation: One-lung ventilation creates marked V/Q inequality and increases alveolar dead space. Poorly perfused ventilated units dilute exhaled CO2, so ETCO2 can substantially underestimate PaCO2 and the arterial-to-end-tidal gradient widens.

questions.stem: During MRI under GA, sidestream capnography shows a delayed, damped waveform and ETCO2 lower than expected. Which setup factor should be considered?
options: Long sampling tubing adds transit time
Magnetic fields raise the patient's CO2 output
questions.explanation: MRI requires long sampling lines so the monitor can sit away from the magnet, and the extra length adds transit time and mixing, so the waveform appears late and damped and ETCO2 may read lower than expected. The trend is still useful. Contrast and the magnetic field do not change CO2 production.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, the inspiratory capnogram baseline rises above zero and the CO2 absorbent is exhausted. Which correction directly addresses the cause?
options: Lower fresh gas flow further to save agent
Replace absorbent and confirm flow and valves
Replace the pulse oximeter probe on the hand
questions.explanation: With exhausted absorbent, exhaled CO2 passes through the canister unchanged and is rebreathed, so the absorbent is replaced; meanwhile higher fresh gas flow washes CO2 out, and the unidirectional valves are checked as a second cause. Lowering flow worsens rebreathing.

questions.stem: ETCO2 rises from 38 to 62 mmHg despite increased minute ventilation; tachycardia and increasing temperature follow. Which process should be treated as a major concern?
options: A partial disconnection at the circuit Y-piece
questions.explanation: If ETCO2 keeps rising despite increased minute ventilation, simple hypoventilation no longer explains it. With tachycardia and rising temperature during anesthesia, markedly increased metabolic CO2 production such as malignant hyperthermia requires urgent consideration. Rebreathing raises the inspired baseline, and esophageal intubation or disconnection lowers ETCO2.

questions.stem: The inspired-O2 analyzer alarms at 18% during GA. Which action has priority?
options: Check the pipeline pressure before changing gas
Increase the volatile concentration to compensate
Wait for SpO2 to fall before changing anything
Deliver a safe oxygen source now, then investigate
questions.explanation: An inspired oxygen of 18% means a hypoxic mixture is reaching the patient, so the first step is a known safe oxygen source, such as opening the cylinder and disconnecting the pipeline if crossover is suspected, or a self-inflating bag on a separate cylinder. The cause is investigated once oxygen delivery is secured.

questions.stem: Immediately after intubation, which monitor is expected to identify persistent esophageal placement before pulse oximetry typically changes?
questions.explanation: Capnography shows esophageal placement within a few breaths because no sustained CO2 returns, while pulse oximetry may stay normal for minutes after preoxygenation, and blood pressure and ECG change only once hypoxemia is advanced. That speed is why capnography is the standard for confirming tube placement.

questions.stem: Five minutes after IV cefazolin, PIP rises with wheezing, BP falls to 70/40, HR is 130/min, and urticaria appears on the chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm with hypotension, tachycardia, and urticaria minutes after an antibiotic is anaphylaxis, and epinephrine is the first drug. Light-anesthesia bronchospasm does not cause shock or skin findings, tension pneumothorax causes unilateral loss of breath sounds without urticaria, and mainstem intubation causes asymmetric sounds rather than wheezing with shock.

questions.stem: After patient repositioning, PIP rises abruptly and breath sounds become absent on the left. Which two diagnoses should be rapidly distinguished?
questions.explanation: Absent breath sounds on one side after repositioning, with a rise in peak pressure, fit either a tube that has slipped into the right mainstem or a left pneumothorax. Checking tube depth and withdrawing the tube distinguishes them quickly; a pneumothorax also brings rising plateau pressure, hypotension, and tracheal shift. Bronchospasm and leaks do not cause one-sided silence.

questions.stem: PIP and exhaled tidal volume fall, but a smaller ETCO2 waveform persists. Which circuit problem is most consistent with this pattern?
options: A complete disconnection at the Y-piece
A partial leak still allowing some ventilation
questions.explanation: A partial leak lets some of each breath escape, so peak pressure and exhaled volume fall, but enough gas still reaches the lungs to produce a smaller capnogram. A complete disconnection or esophageal intubation would abolish the waveform, and bronchospasm raises peak pressure.

questions.stem: Motion artifact repeatedly triggers low-SpO2 alarms during an otherwise stable anesthetic. Which response best preserves safety?
options: Lower the low-SpO2 alarm threshold to 70%
Disable the SpO2 alarm for the rest of the case
Use ETCO2 as the only oxygenation monitor
Fix the probe or source while keeping alarms on
questions.explanation: Motion artifact is managed by fixing the cause, such as securing or moving the probe, using a motion-tolerant sensor, or limiting movement, while keeping alarms on at appropriate limits. Disabling or lowering alarms removes protection against a real desaturation, and ETCO2 does not measure oxygenation.

questions.stem: A clinician lowers the SpO2 alarm threshold to 80% solely to suppress nuisance alarms. Why is this unsafe?
options: Limits must stay appropriate; fix artifact instead
A lower limit produces more nuisance alarms
Lower thresholds make the monitor oversensitive
Changing the limit alters the measured SpO2
questions.explanation: Alarm limits can be individualized, but a low-SpO2 limit of 80% lets clinically important desaturation pass silently, so nuisance alarms are addressed by fixing artifact and checking the patient. A lower limit makes the monitor less sensitive, not more, and does not change the measurement itself.

questions.stem: Where should the tip of an esophageal temperature probe sit for an accurate core temperature reading?
options: In the stomach below the cardia
questions.explanation: An esophageal probe reads core temperature when its tip lies in the lower third of the esophagus, behind the heart, where blood temperature dominates. Placed higher, it is cooled by gas flowing in the trachea, and in the stomach it reads gastric contents and irrigation rather than core temperature.

questions.stem: A capnogram develops a terminal upward deflection near the end of expiration in a patient with inadequate expiratory time and stiff lungs. Which named morphology is this?
questions.explanation: A pigtail capnogram shows a terminal upward hook at the end of expiration when expiratory time is too short for stiff lungs, reflecting incomplete emptying and breath stacking. A curare cleft is a notch from patient effort, a shark fin reflects obstruction, and cardiogenic oscillations are small ripples timed to the heartbeat.

questions.stem: A remote anesthetizing location loses mains power and all non-battery-backed monitors shut down. Which pre-case preparation would most directly reduce this vulnerability?
options: Open the backup oxygen cylinder first
questions.explanation: When mains power fails, only battery-backed monitors, laryngoscopes, and a charged flashlight keep working, so confirming that backup equipment is charged before a remote case most directly reduces the risk. Opening the oxygen cylinder protects against pipeline failure, not power loss, and the vaporizer and water trap do not depend on power.

questions.stem: A high-PEEP alarm activates. Which broad ventilator-alarm category does this belong to?
options: Oxygen analyzer alarms in the inspired limb
questions.explanation: A high PEEP alarm signals end-expiratory pressure above the set limit, which can come from a stuck expiratory valve, scavenger obstruction, or auto-PEEP, so it is a ventilator pressure alarm. Volume and disconnect alarms track delivered and returned gas, and oxygen alarms track inspired concentration.

questions.stem: On an older ventilator without fresh gas decoupling, raising fresh gas flow from 2 to 8 L/min increases exhaled tidal volume. Why?
options: Inspiratory fresh gas adds to each breath
The bellows leaks less at higher flows
Higher flow raises the lungs' compliance
The flow sensor reads high from humidity
questions.explanation: On ventilators without fresh gas decoupling, gas entering the circuit during inspiration adds to the bellows volume. Adding 6 L/min at 10 breaths per minute with an I:E of 1:2 adds about 6000/10 x 1/3, or roughly 200 mL per breath. Modern machines decouple or compensate for fresh gas, and lung compliance does not change with flow.

questions.stem: At the end of surgery, the quantitative TOF ratio is 0.7. The patient is breathing spontaneously and sustains a 5-second head lift. Should the patient be extubated now?
options: Yes, since head lift shows full recovery
Not yet; wait for a ratio of at least 0.9
Yes, since 0.7 is adequate for extubation
No, wait for four equal twitches by eye
questions.explanation: Pharyngeal and upper airway weakness persists below a TOF ratio of 0.9, raising aspiration and hypoxemia risk, so extubation waits for 0.9 or more on a quantitative monitor or further reversal is given. A head lift and visually equal twitches can both occur at ratios well below 0.9.

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 remains elevated after fresh absorbent is installed. Which circuit causes should be evaluated next?
options: Exhausted absorbent in the new canister
Valve dysfunction or low fresh gas flow
questions.explanation: With fresh absorbent installed, persistent inspired CO2 comes from an incompetent inspiratory or expiratory unidirectional valve or fresh gas flow too low for the circuit, and an analyzer zero error should also be checked. Fever raises end-tidal, not inspired, CO2, and esophageal intubation removes the waveform.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 20 mmHg while simultaneous PaCO2 is 40 mmHg and a sustained waveform is present. Which physiologic explanation is most likely?
options: CO2 rebreathing from the breathing circuit
More dead space or less pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: PaCO2 reflects arterial CO2, whereas ETCO2 reflects gas from ventilated alveoli. A 20 mmHg gap with a sustained waveform means a large share of ventilation goes to poorly perfused or unperfused alveoli, as with increased dead space or low pulmonary blood flow. Hypoventilation raises both values without widening the gap.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly falls to 10 mmHg while severe hypotension and bradycardia develop. Which category of problem is most concerning?
options: Loss of pulmonary perfusion from arrest or embolism
Sampling artifact despite the hemodynamic collapse
CO2 rebreathing from an exhausted absorbent canister
questions.explanation: A sudden fall in ETCO2 to 10 mmHg together with severe hypotension and bradycardia means little blood is reaching the lungs, as in impending arrest or massive embolism, so circulatory support starts at once. Calling it artifact during visible collapse delays resuscitation, rebreathing raises CO2, and bronchospasm does not drop ETCO2 this far.

questions.stem: ETCO2 gradually rises with a preserved waveform and unchanged ventilator settings. Which causes belong highest on the initial differential?
options: Reduced alveolar ventilation or increased CO2 production
A sudden increase in dead space from cardiovascular collapse
questions.explanation: A gradual ETCO2 rise with a preserved waveform and unchanged ventilator settings means less CO2 is being removed or more is being produced, as with fever, sepsis, CO2 insufflation, or a hypermetabolic state. Disconnection and esophageal intubation abolish the waveform, and cardiovascular collapse lowers ETCO2.

questions.stem: During intraoperative bronchospasm with rising auto-PEEP, which ventilator adjustment best limits air trapping?
options: Higher rate to clear the rising CO2 quickly
Lower rate with a longer expiratory time
Higher PEEP to keep small airways open
Shorter expiratory time with larger breaths
questions.explanation: During bronchospasm, expiratory flow is slow, so a lower rate and a lower I:E ratio give the lungs time to empty and limit air trapping and auto-PEEP, accepting some permissive hypercapnia. Faster rates and shorter expiratory times worsen trapping, and high external PEEP can add to hyperinflation.

questions.stem: Several hours into a case, peak pressure has climbed slowly while plateau pressure is stable. A suction catheter passes freely through the tube, and the HME at the Y-piece looks wet. What is the most likely cause?
options: A saturated HME filter adding resistance
A kinked tube at the bite block
questions.explanation: A heat and moisture exchanger saturated with water, secretions, or blood adds resistance at the Y-piece, so peak pressure climbs gradually with a stable plateau while a suction catheter still passes freely through the tube. Replacing the HME fixes it. Reduced compliance would raise the plateau, and a kink would stop the catheter.

questions.stem: The inspiratory capnogram baseline remains above zero despite adequate fresh-gas flow. Which causes should be investigated?
options: Low cardiac output causing CO2 rebreathing
Valve dysfunction or an analyzer zero error
questions.explanation: Persistent inspired CO2 despite adequate fresh gas flow suggests rebreathing from an incompetent unidirectional valve or an analyzer zero or calibration problem. Pulmonary embolism, hypovolemia, and low cardiac output lower end-tidal CO2 and do not put CO2 into inspired gas.

questions.stem: During cemented arthroplasty, ETCO2 suddenly falls from 36 to 20 mmHg with a preserved waveform and simultaneous hypotension. Which physiologic event is most concerning?
questions.explanation: An abrupt fall in ETCO2 with a preserved waveform and hypotension during cemented arthroplasty points to reduced pulmonary blood flow from fat, cement, or air embolism, which raises dead space. A sampling problem distorts the waveform, rebreathing raises baseline CO2, and a ventilation change lowers ETCO2 gradually without hypotension.

questions.stem: After head rotation, ETCO2 and SpO2 both fall and breath sounds become markedly asymmetric. Which airway problem should be evaluated immediately?
options: Tube migration or kink from the head turn
Cuff inflating on the oximeter arm
questions.explanation: Head rotation can push the tube into a mainstem bronchus or kink it; falling SpO2 and ETCO2 with markedly asymmetric breath sounds call for immediate assessment of tube depth and patency. Methemoglobinemia, cuff interference, and carbon monoxide do not produce asymmetric breath sounds.

questions.stem: SpO2 falls while FiO2 and ETCO2 remain unchanged and ventilation appears adequate. Which problem category should move higher on the differential?
options: An oxygenation problem such as shunt
questions.explanation: Falling SpO2 with stable FiO2, ETCO2, and ventilation points toward an oxygenation problem such as atelectasis, shunt, or V/Q mismatch rather than a ventilation or equipment problem. Hypoventilation would raise ETCO2, and rebreathing raises the inspired baseline.

questions.stem: SpO2 abruptly falls when electrocautery begins, but the pleth waveform simultaneously becomes erratic and the patient otherwise appears unchanged. What is the best first response?
options: Treat severe hypoxemia based on the number
Diagnose CO2 rebreathing from the circuit
Check the patient and probe for cautery artifact
questions.explanation: Electrocautery can distort pulse oximeter signals, and an erratic pleth timed to cautery use with an otherwise unchanged patient points to artifact. The patient and waveform are assessed before treating an isolated abrupt saturation change as true hypoxemia.

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry becomes unreliable in a severely hypothermic, vasoconstricted patient. What technical limitation is responsible?
options: Loss of a usable pulsatile perfusion signal
Light from warming lamps blinding the probe
questions.explanation: Severe hypothermia causes intense peripheral vasoconstriction and weak pulsatile flow, shrinking the signal pulse oximetry requires. A central site such as the ear or forehead often works better. Cold does not form methemoglobin, and anemia does not prevent signal detection.

questions.stem: During major hemorrhage, SpO2 is 99% and hemoglobin is 9 g/dL, but mixed venous O2 saturation falls from 75% to 50%. What does this indicate?
options: Tissues are failing to extract oxygen
Oxygen delivery is not meeting demand
Pulse oximetry is reading falsely high
questions.explanation: A low mixed venous saturation means tissues are extracting more oxygen than usual because delivery, set by cardiac output, hemoglobin, and SaO2, is inadequate for demand, as with bleeding and falling cardiac output. Impaired extraction, as in sepsis or cyanide toxicity, and falling consumption both raise SvO2.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient has SpO2 99% despite headache and confusion. Which measurement is needed to evaluate the suspected dyshemoglobinemia?
questions.explanation: Standard pulse oximeters use two wavelengths and read carboxyhemoglobin as if it were oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 stays falsely high after smoke exposure. Multiwavelength co-oximetry on a blood sample separates COHb from O2Hb and is the test that confirms the diagnosis. Repeating the same oximeter only repeats the same error, and ETCO2 says nothing about hemoglobin species.

questions.stem: After topical benzocaine, SpO2 stabilizes near 85% despite supplemental oxygen and PaO2 is adequate. Which dyshemoglobinemia should be suspected?
options: Sulfhemoglobinemia as the expected benzocaine effect
No dyshemoglobinemia because PaO2 is adequate
questions.explanation: Benzocaine is a classic trigger for methemoglobinemia. Because MetHb absorbs both red and infrared light about equally, the oximeter drifts toward roughly 85% regardless of the true saturation, while PaO2 stays normal because it measures dissolved oxygen, not hemoglobin binding. A normal PaO2 therefore does not exclude a dyshemoglobinemia; co-oximetry confirms it.

questions.stem: Which fingernail polish color is most likely to falsely lower a pulse oximeter reading?
questions.explanation: Dark polishes, especially blue, black, and green, absorb light near 660 nm and can falsely lower SpO2, while red, pale, and clear polishes have little effect. Removing the polish or turning the probe sideways across the finger restores accuracy.

questions.stem: A profoundly anemic patient has SpO2 100% but shows evidence of inadequate oxygen delivery. Why is the saturation alone reassuring only about one component of oxygen content?
options: Anemia causes standard pulse oximeters to report hematocrit
SpO2 directly measures total arterial oxygen content
SpO2 reflects hemoglobin saturation but not the amount of hemoglobin available to carry oxygen
A saturation of 100% guarantees normal oxygen delivery regardless of hemoglobin concentration
questions.explanation: SpO2 is the percentage of available hemoglobin carrying oxygen. Arterial oxygen content depends mostly on hemoglobin concentration times saturation, so a patient with very low hemoglobin can be 100% saturated and still have poor oxygen content and delivery. The oximeter does not measure hemoglobin or cardiac output.

questions.stem: What is the approximate P50 of normal adult hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: P50, the PO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated, is about 26 to 27 mmHg for normal adult hemoglobin. A higher P50 means a right shift and lower affinity, while fetal hemoglobin has a P50 near 19 mmHg. A PO2 of 40 corresponds to about 75% saturation, the normal mixed venous value, and 60 to about 90%.

questions.stem: Alkalosis, hypocapnia, and hypothermia shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left. What is the principal consequence?
options: Higher affinity with less unloading to tissue
Lower affinity with more unloading to tissue
No change in hemoglobin oxygen affinity
Lower arterial saturation at every PaO2
questions.explanation: Alkalosis, hypocapnia, hypothermia, and reduced 2,3-DPG shift the curve to the left. Hemoglobin then holds oxygen more tightly, so saturation can look good while less oxygen is released to tissue. This is the reverse of the right-shift pattern and one reason aggressive hyperventilation is not benign.

questions.stem: A patient has hemoglobin 10 g/dL, SaO2 98%, and PaO2 100 mmHg. What is the approximate arterial oxygen content?
questions.explanation: CaO2 = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2) = (1.34 x 10 x 0.98) + (0.003 x 100) = 13.1 + 0.3, about 13.4 mL/dL. Dissolved oxygen adds very little, so hemoglobin concentration drives content; a normal hemoglobin of 15 g/dL would give about 19.8 mL/dL.

questions.stem: A radial arterial catheter is desired, but the proposed wrist has cellulitis while the contralateral site is usable. Which choice best balances monitoring need and procedural risk?
options: Proceed at that site if the Allen test is normal
Cannulate the infected site after antibiotics
Use an alternative uninfected arterial site
Skip arterial monitoring and use NIBP alone
questions.explanation: Local infection is a contraindication to arterial cannulation at that site because the catheter can seed the bloodstream, so an uninfected site such as the other radial artery is used. A normal Allen test does not address infection, antibiotics do not make the site safe, and abandoning arterial monitoring gives up a needed monitor when a safe site exists.

questions.stem: A previously normal radial arterial waveform becomes flat and the catheter no longer flushes, while ECG and pulse oximetry show continued circulation. Which technical problem is most likely?
questions.explanation: A flat arterial trace that will not flush, while the ECG and pleth show ongoing circulation, means the catheter or tubing is clotted, kinked, or occluded. Asystole would flatten the pleth too, a low transducer raises the reading without flattening it, and underdamping exaggerates rather than abolishes the waveform.

questions.stem: A patient in complete heart block has a CVP trace with intermittent, very large waves that coincide with atrial contraction. What are these waves?
questions.explanation: Cannon a waves occur when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, as in complete heart block, junctional rhythm, or ventricular pacing, producing intermittent large a waves. Large v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation, and absent a waves suggest atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: A CVP trace shows tall waves during ventricular systole that merge with the c wave and erase the x descent. Which condition best explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: In tricuspid regurgitation, blood flows back into the right atrium during systole, producing tall v waves that fuse with the c wave and erase the x descent. Complete heart block causes cannon a waves, atrial fibrillation removes a waves, and constrictive pericarditis gives steep x and y descents with an M or W shape.

questions.stem: A NIBP cuff cycles every minute on the same arm for hours despite stable hemodynamics. Which preventable complication becomes more likely?
options: Systematic falsely low pressure from repeated inflation
Deep venous thrombosis of the upper extremity
Compression-related nerve injury or compartment syndrome
Brachial artery dissection from cuff pressure
questions.explanation: Hours of cuff inflation every minute on one arm can compress nerves and cause edema, petechiae, and compartment syndrome, so the cycling interval should be lengthened or the cuff site rotated. Repeated inflation does not make readings systematically low, and venous thrombosis or arterial dissection from a correctly sized cuff is not the expected injury.

questions.stem: A precordial Doppler is placed to detect venous air embolism during a sitting craniotomy. Where should it be positioned?
options: Left midclavicular line over the apex
Over the suprasternal notch and trachea
Left sternal border at the 2nd interspace
questions.explanation: A precordial Doppler is placed over the right heart, usually at the right sternal border between the third and sixth intercostal spaces, and position is confirmed by a change in sound when saline is injected through a central line. It detects very small amounts of air, second only to TEE, while apical or left-sided placement samples the left heart.

questions.stem: Why is thermodilution cardiac output unreliable in a patient with severe tricuspid regurgitation?
options: Regurgitant flow distorts the indicator curve
Cold injectate cannot enter the right atrium
The thermistor sits in the wrong ventricle
TR raises blood temperature in the PA
questions.explanation: Thermodilution assumes the cold indicator passes once through the right heart to the thermistor in the pulmonary artery; with severe TR, part of it washes back and forth across the valve, prolonging and flattening the curve and making the calculated output inaccurate. Intracardiac shunts cause similar errors.

questions.stem: Oscillometric NIBP values vary widely in atrial fibrillation despite correct cuff size and position. Which feature of the rhythm explains the reduced reliability?
options: AF directly raises the pressure inside the cuff
AF makes each reading falsely high by 20 mmHg
AF prevents the cuff from deflating properly
questions.explanation: In atrial fibrillation, stroke volume and pulse pressure change from beat to beat, so the cuff oscillations the device analyzes are irregular and readings vary or fail. Repeating and averaging measurements, or using an arterial line, gives a better estimate. AF does not raise cuff pressure or prevent deflation.

questions.stem: During vascular surgery, new horizontal ST depression develops in a monitored precordial lead during tachycardia and hypotension. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Assume electrode error without seeing the patient
Dismiss it, as ST depression is common under GA
Treat as ischemia, fix supply-demand, verify signal
Drop the precordial lead and watch lead II alone
questions.explanation: New horizontal ST depression in a precordial lead during tachycardia and hypotension in a vascular patient is presumed demand ischemia, so heart rate is slowed and pressure restored while the signal is checked. Dismissing it or removing the lead that shows it loses the warning.

questions.stem: With high PEEP and relative hypovolemia, a pulmonary artery catheter tip lies where alveolar pressure exceeds pulmonary venous pressure. What does the occlusion pressure now reflect?
options: Left atrial pressure with improved accuracy
Right atrial pressure transmitted across the lung
Alveolar pressure rather than left atrial pressure
questions.explanation: PAOP reflects left atrial pressure only when a continuous column of blood links the catheter tip to the left atrium, as in West zone 3. If the tip sits where alveolar pressure exceeds pulmonary venous pressure, as with high PEEP or hypovolemia, the reading reflects alveolar pressure and overestimates left atrial pressure.

questions.stem: A patient with significant CAD is monitored with only a basic 3-lead configuration. What important limitation remains despite adequate rhythm detection?
options: Low sensitivity for ischemia across territories
It cannot detect atrial arrhythmias at all
It cannot display a reliable heart rate count
It cannot show an ST change in its displayed lead
questions.explanation: A 3-electrode system shows one limb lead at a time, which detects rhythm well but misses ischemia in territories it does not view, especially the anterolateral wall seen in V3 to V5. ST changes in the displayed lead still appear, so the limitation is coverage, not detection within that lead.

questions.stem: After a warming blanket is removed, the ECG shows a chaotic fine baseline in all leads while the arterial line and pleth show regular pulses at 80/min. What is the most likely explanation?
options: New atrial fibrillation with rapid response
Artifact; the heart is perfusing normally
Torsades de pointes triggered by cold
questions.explanation: A chaotic ECG baseline with regular arterial and pleth waveforms at a normal rate means the heart is beating normally and the ECG is picking up artifact, here likely from shivering. Ventricular fibrillation would abolish the arterial pulse, and atrial fibrillation would make pulses irregular. Checking a second monitor before acting prevents shocking a perfusing rhythm.

questions.stem: A preinduction ECG strip is normal, but new ST depression appears after surgical stimulation. What is the principal value of the baseline tracing?
options: It calibrates the ECG monitor amplitude
It completes all later ischemia assessment
It shows whether the change is new
questions.explanation: A baseline strip shows the patient's own ST segments, T waves, and conduction before anesthesia, so changes after stimulation can be judged as new rather than chronic. It does not calibrate the monitor or replace a diagnostic 12-lead ECG, and later changes still need assessment.

questions.stem: New ST depression appears with tachycardia and hypotension in a patient with CAD. Which immediate physiologic goal best addresses myocardial oxygen balance?
options: Lower demand and restore perfusion pressure
Remove the precordial lead showing the change
Wait for ST elevation before intervening
questions.explanation: Myocardial oxygen balance improves by slowing the heart, which lengthens diastolic coronary filling and lowers demand, and by restoring diastolic pressure and oxygen supply. Deepening anesthesia blindly may worsen hypotension, and most perioperative ischemia never progresses to ST elevation.

questions.stem: During GA, distal esophageal temperature is 35.2 °C while exposed-skin temperature is 33 °C. Which value more closely represents core temperature?
options: An equal average of the two
Neither unless a pulmonary-artery catheter is present
questions.explanation: The distal esophagus reflects core temperature because it lies next to the heart and great vessels, while exposed skin is cooled by the room and reads several degrees lower. Mean body temperature weights core about 0.85, so an equal average misstates it, and a pulmonary artery catheter is not required to estimate core temperature.

questions.stem: After rewarming on bypass to a nasopharyngeal temperature of 37 C, core temperature falls to 35.5 C over the first hour in the ICU. What best explains this?
options: Malfunction of the bladder temperature probe
Afterdrop as heat moves to the cooler periphery
Early sepsis lowering the set point
Heat loss from cold ICU air by itself
questions.explanation: During rapid rewarming on bypass, the core warms faster than peripheral tissues, so once warming stops, heat flows from the core into the still-cool periphery and core temperature falls again, called afterdrop. Slower rewarming, warming to a higher peripheral temperature, and forced-air warming afterward reduce it.

questions.stem: Late in a volatile anesthetic, ETCO2 rises despite increased ventilation, tachycardia develops, and core temperature then begins to increase. Which diagnosis requires immediate consideration?
options: Forced-air warming as the sole explanation
questions.explanation: In malignant hyperthermia, hypercarbia despite increased ventilation and unexplained tachycardia appear first, and temperature rises later, so this sequence fits MH. Stopping volatile agents, giving dantrolene, and hyperventilating with 100% oxygen begin immediately. Infection, routine fever, and forced-air warming do not cause hypercarbia that resists increased ventilation.

questions.stem: A patient reaches 34.5 °C after a long operation. Which pair of effects is most consistent with clinically significant perioperative hypothermia?
options: Lower oxygen demand during postoperative shivering
Reduced infection risk and faster metabolism
Impaired coagulation and prolonged drug effects
questions.explanation: Mild hypothermia impairs platelet function and coagulation enzymes, increasing blood loss, and slows hepatic metabolism and Hofmann elimination, prolonging neuromuscular blockers and other drugs. Shivering raises rather than lowers oxygen consumption, and hypothermia increases wound infection risk and slows emergence.

questions.stem: Core temperature falls most rapidly soon after induction even before prolonged environmental exposure. Which mechanism is especially important in this early phase?
options: Higher metabolic heat production after induction
Evaporative heat loss through the lungs
Redistribution of core heat to the periphery
Conductive loss through the IV tubing
questions.explanation: General anesthesia impairs normal vasoconstriction and thermoregulatory control, so heat stored in the core redistributes into cooler peripheral tissues, and core temperature falls 1 to 1.5 C in the first hour before environmental losses dominate. Metabolic heat production falls rather than rises under anesthesia, and respiratory and IV tubing losses are small.

questions.stem: Which intervention is most effective at preventing intraoperative hypothermia in adults?
options: Warming IV fluids at maintenance rates
questions.explanation: Forced-air warming transfers heat across a large skin surface and is the most effective common method, and prewarming before induction reduces redistribution hypothermia. Warming fluids matters mainly when large volumes are given, airway humidification adds little heat, and passive cotton blankets reduce loss only modestly.

questions.stem: A patient is shivering vigorously in PACU after a long case. Which drug is most effective for stopping postoperative shivering?
questions.explanation: Meperidine, about 12.5 to 25 mg IV, stops shivering more effectively than equianalgesic doses of other opioids, likely through kappa-receptor and alpha-2 effects on the shivering threshold. Fentanyl and morphine are tempting because they are opioids, but they are much less effective at equianalgesic doses, and midazolam does not reliably stop shivering.

questions.stem: During a long case under full forced-air warming, temperature climbs to 38.3 C while ETCO2, heart rate, and minute ventilation stay at baseline. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: A rising temperature with stable ETCO2, heart rate, and ventilation points to too much external heat rather than a hypermetabolic state, so the warmer setting is lowered and coverage reduced. Thyroid storm, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and sepsis raise CO2 production and heart rate, which are absent here.

questions.stem: The OR line isolation monitor alarms at 5 mA right after a new device is plugged in. What is the appropriate first response?
options: Unplug the most recently connected device
Shut off all room power immediately
Ignore it, since the patient is grounded
Silence the alarm and continue the case
questions.explanation: The line isolation monitor alarms when the isolated power system has developed a path to ground large enough to allow a hazardous current, often from a faulty device just plugged in. Unplugging the most recently connected equipment usually clears it. The alarm does not mean the patient is being shocked, so cutting all power is unnecessary, but ignoring it leaves a first fault in place.

questions.stem: During positive-pressure ventilation, at what point in the respiratory cycle should CVP be read?
questions.explanation: Intrathoracic pressure is closest to atmospheric at end-expiration, so CVP and other intrathoracic vascular pressures are read then to minimize the effect of airway pressure. During positive-pressure inspiration, intrathoracic pressure rises and CVP reads falsely high, and averaging blends that error in.

questions.stem: A small air bubble enters arterial-pressure tubing and the waveform becomes rounded. Which measurement effect is expected?
options: A higher dicrotic notch with accurate systolic pressure
questions.explanation: An air bubble adds compliance to the fluid column, which increases damping, so the waveform rounds, the dicrotic notch fades, and systolic pressure reads low while MAP is less affected. Underdamping would exaggerate systolic pressure instead.

questions.stem: An arterial line is connected through long compliant tubing with multiple stopcocks. Why can the displayed waveform become misleading?
options: Long tubing changes only the zero point
Extra tubing raises the natural frequency
Stopcocks prevent damping of the waveform
questions.explanation: Long compliant tubing and multiple stopcocks lower the natural frequency and alter damping, so the displayed waveform can overshoot or flatten and systolic and diastolic values become unreliable. Short, stiff tubing with few connections preserves fidelity.

questions.stem: Fast-flush release produces one oscillation followed by a crisp arterial waveform with a visible dicrotic notch. How should the dynamic response be interpreted?
questions.explanation: One oscillation after the fast flush followed by a crisp waveform with a visible dicrotic notch shows near-optimal damping, so displayed systolic, diastolic, and mean pressures are reliable. Several oscillations mean underdamping, and a slow return without oscillation means overdamping or occlusion.

questions.stem: In beach-chair position, a radial arterial transducer is leveled at the right atrium and displays MAP 70 mmHg. Why may cerebral arterial pressure be lower?
options: Upright position makes the transducer read low
Radial MAP always underestimates brain pressure
ETCO2 sets the whole heart-to-brain difference
The brain sits above the heart, lowering its pressure
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure falls with height above the reference point. In the beach-chair position the brain sits well above the heart, so a MAP measured with the transducer at the right atrium overstates the pressure actually present at cerebral level, by about 0.75 mmHg per centimeter.

questions.stem: A distal arterial site displays higher systolic pressure and wider pulse pressure than a more central site while MAP is similar. Which phenomenon best explains this?
options: Hydrostatic leveling error at the distal site
Overdamping in the more distal catheter
questions.explanation: Distal arteries show higher systolic and wider pulse pressure because reflected pressure waves from branching, tapering vessels add to the forward wave, while MAP stays about the same. Overdamping lowers systolic pressure, and a hydrostatic error shifts MAP as well.

questions.stem: A patient requires continuous norepinephrine titration and frequent arterial blood gases during major surgery. Which monitor best serves both purposes?
questions.explanation: An arterial catheter gives beat-to-beat pressure for titrating norepinephrine and a site for repeated arterial blood gases, which no noninvasive monitor provides. A central line can sample venous blood and deliver norepinephrine but does not measure arterial pressure, and NIBP and finger-cuff devices cannot provide arterial samples.

questions.stem: Major thoracic surgery with one-lung ventilation is expected to involve rapid hemodynamic changes and repeated blood-gas assessment. Which pressure-monitoring strategy is most appropriate?
options: The pulse oximeter waveform by itself
ECG with no added pressure monitoring
questions.explanation: One-lung ventilation and major thoracic surgery bring rapid hemodynamic changes from surgical compression and bleeding plus a need for repeated blood gases, so a continuous arterial line is standard. A 10-minute NIBP interval is below the minimum standard, and the pleth or ECG cannot measure pressure.

questions.stem: In septic shock on high-dose norepinephrine, radial MAP reads 55 mmHg. What is the main concern about relying on this value?
options: It cannot be read while vasopressors run
It reflects venous rather than arterial pressure
It may underestimate central arterial pressure
questions.explanation: With intense vasoconstriction from high-dose vasopressors, radial artery pressure can fall below aortic or femoral pressure, so a radial MAP of 55 may understate central pressure and lead to excess vasopressor. A femoral line gives a more central reading when the gap matters. Peripheral amplification raises distal systolic pressure, but vasoconstriction can lower distal MAP.

questions.stem: To what pressure is an arterial line flush bag usually inflated?
questions.explanation: The flush bag is pressurized to about 300 mmHg, above arterial pressure, so the flush device delivers a continuous 2 to 3 mL/hr and blood cannot back up into the tubing. At 100 to 150 mmHg, arterial pressure can exceed bag pressure during hypertension and blood refluxes, risking clot and damping.

questions.stem: An arterial waveform develops a slow upstroke, reduced amplitude, and loss of its dicrotic notch while NIBP remains stable. What should be checked first?
options: Assume the displayed systolic pressure is accurate
Overdamping from air, clot, kinking, or excessive tubing
questions.explanation: A slow upstroke, smaller amplitude, and lost dicrotic notch with a stable cuff pressure point to overdamping from air, clot, a kink, or excess tubing, so the system is checked before trusting the low systolic value. Raising the transducer would lower all values without changing the waveform's shape.

questions.stem: The hand distal to a radial arterial catheter becomes cold, pale, and poorly perfused. Which complication requires prompt evaluation?
options: Radial nerve injury from the stick
questions.explanation: A cold, pale, poorly perfused hand distal to a radial catheter suggests thrombosis or embolism with ischemia, so the catheter is removed and perfusion reassessed, with vascular consultation if it does not recover. Nerve injury causes numbness without pallor, and cuff injury affects the cuffed limb rather than the hand below the catheter.

questions.stem: A pressurized arterial-line flush bag empties and the continuous flush stops. Which technical complication becomes more likely over time?
options: Zero drift producing falsely high readings
Catheter clotting with loss of the waveform
questions.explanation: The continuous flush, about 3 mL/hr, keeps blood from clotting at the catheter tip; once the bag empties, flow stops and the catheter clots, damping and then losing the waveform. Zero drift is a transducer problem unrelated to flush flow, and an empty bag reduces flow rather than causing underdamping.

questions.stem: Before radial cannulation, the radial artery is compressed while the pleth on the thumb is watched. What does a persistent pleth waveform indicate?
options: The radial artery is too small to cannulate
Ulnar collateral flow to the hand
The ulnar artery is occluded on that side
Radial cannulation will carry no ischemic risk
questions.explanation: A persistent pleth on the thumb during radial compression shows that ulnar and palmar arch collaterals perfuse the hand, a more objective version of the Allen test. It does not guarantee freedom from ischemia, and loss of the waveform would suggest poor collateral flow.

questions.stem: After forceful pressurized flushing of a radial arterial catheter, the hand becomes painful, pale, and poorly perfused. Which complication is most concerning?
options: Distal ischemia from embolism or injury
Median nerve irritation from the flush
questions.explanation: Forceful pressurized flushing can drive air or clot distally and injure the artery, so a painful, pale, poorly perfused hand afterward points to distal ischemia from embolism or thrombosis. Reactive hyperemia would make the hand red rather than pale, and nerve irritation does not cause pallor. Gentle, small-volume flushes prevent it.

questions.stem: A patient becomes profoundly hypotensive shortly after induction between routine 5-minute NIBP measurements. Which monitoring change would best reduce the chance of missing another rapid episode?
options: Shorter cycling or an arterial line when indicated
Lengthen the NIBP interval to reduce cuff trauma
Add processed EEG in place of pressure readings
Move the cuff to the opposite arm
questions.explanation: Routine 5-minute NIBP cycling can miss brief but clinically important pressure changes during unstable periods, so the interval should be shortened or an arterial line placed when beat-to-beat data are needed. Moving the cuff changes the site but not how often pressure is sampled, and processed EEG does not measure blood pressure.

questions.stem: A patient with limited cardiovascular reserve undergoes major surgery with anticipated rapid blood loss and vasoactive titration. Which BP-monitoring approach is most appropriate?
options: Routine NIBP every 10 minutes after induction
Invasive pressure or much more frequent readings
Stop blood pressure checks after induction
Check pressure after major surgical events
questions.explanation: Limited cardiovascular reserve, rapid blood loss, and vasoactive titration call for beat-to-beat arterial pressure or, at minimum, much more frequent cuff readings, because hypotension can cause ischemia within minutes. Ten-minute cycling violates the 5-minute minimum, and checking only after surgical events misses the swings between them.

questions.stem: NIBP reads 88/50 mmHg while the cuffed arm is elevated well above the heart and the patient otherwise appears stable. What should be done before treating the number?
options: Accept it, since cuff height has no effect
Level the cuff to the heart and repeat it
Stop monitoring until the patient is supine
questions.explanation: A cuff on an arm well above the heart reads lower than heart-level pressure by about 0.75 mmHg per centimeter of height, so the arm is brought to heart level, or the offset accounted for, and the pressure repeated before a vasopressor is given to a stable-appearing patient. Treating an artifact exposes the patient to an unneeded pressor.

questions.stem: An NIBP cuff is wrapped over a thick sweater sleeve. How is the reading likely affected?
options: Falsely low from extra compression of the artery
Unaffected, since oscillations pass through cloth
Accurate for MAP but low for systolic
Falsely high from poor pressure transmission
questions.explanation: Thick clothing under the cuff absorbs and dampens pressure, so more cuff pressure is needed to compress the artery and readings tend to run high and become erratic; the cuff should sit on bare skin or a thin sleeve. Clothing does not compress the artery more than bare skin.

questions.stem: During moderate-to-deep propofol sedation for colonoscopy, SpO2, ECG, and NIBP are monitored but exhaled CO2 is not. Which important safety capability is missing?
options: Continuous exhaled CO2 plus clinical observation
Continuous core temperature at a central site
Beat-to-beat pressure from an arterial line
Processed EEG to track the propofol depth
questions.explanation: During moderate or deep sedation, ASA standards require ventilation to be assessed by clinical signs and continuous exhaled CO2 unless precluded, because oximetry on supplemental oxygen detects hypoventilation late. Temperature, invasive pressure, and processed EEG are added by indication.

questions.stem: An awake patient receives an interscalene block without sedation and communicates normally throughout. What ventilation assessment is appropriate under the stated monitoring standard?
options: Mandatory continuous capnography in every unsedated regional anesthetic
Continual observation of qualitative clinical signs of ventilation
questions.explanation: With minimal or no sedation, ASA standards require continual observation of qualitative clinical signs of ventilation, and an awake patient talking normally is clearly ventilating. Capnography becomes expected once moderate or deep sedation is given, and blood gases or transcutaneous CO2 are not routine. Phrenic nerve block from the interscalene approach is still watched for.

questions.stem: During GA, the only CRNA in the room leaves while surgery continues and no one takes over care. Which fundamental monitoring principle is violated?
questions.explanation: ASA Standard I requires qualified anesthesia personnel to be present in the room throughout every general anesthetic, regional anesthetic, and monitored anesthesia care. ECG display, oxygenation checks, and audible capnography alarms are all Standard II requirements, but none of them is what is violated when no qualified provider is in the room.

questions.stem: Under ASA monitoring standards, when pulse oximetry is used during anesthesia, which feature must be audible?
options: A variable-pitch tone and low SpO2 alarm
A fixed-pitch beep at a constant volume
A visual alert with the sound turned off
A tone only when SpO2 falls below 90%
questions.explanation: ASA standards require that when pulse oximetry is used, the variable-pitch pulse tone and the low-threshold alarm be audible to the anesthesia provider, so a falling saturation is heard without looking at the screen. A fixed-pitch beep gives rate but not saturation, and a visual-only alert can be missed.

questions.stem: During mechanical ventilation, the capnography waveform remains displayed but its audible alarm is intentionally silenced for the rest of the case. Why is this unsafe?
options: The alarm matters just during intubation
A displayed trace cannot warn when no one looks
Silencing makes the ETCO2 number inaccurate
Capnography alarms matter mostly during MAC
questions.explanation: ASA standards require the ETCO2 alarm to be audible when capnography is used, because a displayed waveform helps only while someone is looking at it; disconnection or apnea while attention is on the field is detected by sound. Silencing it does not change the measurement, only the warning.

questions.stem: Mechanical ventilation continues after the ventilator's low-pressure alarm is disabled. Which safety layer has been lost?
options: Low inspired O2 alarm on the analyzer
questions.explanation: During mechanical ventilation, ASA standards require a device that detects breathing-system disconnection and sounds an audible alarm. The oxygen analyzer, pulse oximeter, and capnograph remain active, and capnography may eventually show a disconnect, but the specific dedicated audible disconnect detection is what has been lost.

questions.stem: Rocuronium is used and reversal is given without any objective assessment of neuromuscular recovery. Which monitoring problem is most important?
options: Neostigmine will be ineffective without monitoring
A sustained head lift would have been sufficient
questions.explanation: Clinical signs alone miss residual neuromuscular weakness after rocuronium, and reversal given without monitoring may be too early or underdosed, leaving a TOF ratio below 0.9. A head lift can be sustained at TOF ratios well below 0.9, so it is not sufficient, and neostigmine still works without monitoring but its adequacy is unknown.

questions.stem: The workstation functioned normally for an earlier case, so the next anesthetic begins without verifying equipment function. Which safety principle is violated?
options: Recheck equipment just after a malfunction
An earlier good case covers later ones
Recheck the vaporizer and nothing else
questions.explanation: AANA and ASA practice require verifying anesthesia equipment before each anesthetic, with the full checkout at the start of the day and an abbreviated check between cases, because circuits, absorbent, and supplies change between patients. A prior uneventful case does not confirm the setup for the next one.

questions.stem: A cooperative 3-year-old tolerates pulse oximetry before mask induction. Why is obtaining the preinduction value useful?
options: Gives a baseline for judging later changes
